
#### 5.2.1 The Progress Widget

The progress display is the Progress class (Utilities/progress.h/.cpp), a self-contained container widget held by MW::progress and added to the status bar. It replaced the older ProgressBar (removed). Progress does not reference MW: it owns its pixmaps, width, colours and palette and talks to MW only through public methods and the heightChanged() / clicked() signals, so it could be reparented into a standalone window unchanged.

- Rows. Progress holds any number of rows, each with a text column and a bar column, its own bar height, colour, font and Fill style, and its own bar pixmap (so an incremental paint, such as the moving cache cursor, touches only that row).
- addRow(name, barHeight, color, fill) returns an int id; the owner drives the row with updateProgress(id, item, items, color) / clearProgress(id). Fill::FromStart fills 0 -> the current item (sequential progress: FocusStack, RawDenoise); Fill::Cell paints only the current item's cell (items that complete out of order: MetaRead across threads). An invalid colour defaults to the row's bar colour. clearProgress refills the bar background and hides the row.
- The ImageCache row is the exception: its moving cursor and directional range fills are not expressible as a Fill, so Progress creates it in its constructor and keeps its own updateImageCacheProgress() / updateCursor() / clearImageCacheProgress(). Its id is exposed via imageCacheRow() for MW's gate.
- MW adds the other rows at startup in MW::createDataModel: MetaRead "Metadata" (4 px, Fill::Cell), FocusStack "Focus Stack" (2 px, Fill::FromStart) and RawDenoise "Raw Denoise" (2 px, Fill::FromStart), storing their ids in progressMetaReadRow / progressFocusStackRow / progressRawDenoiseRow. Labels default to empty; setRowText() sets them.
- Visibility. All rows start hidden and show only while active, so before a folder is selected the container is empty. updateProgress shows a row and clearProgress hides it; the ImageCache row is revealed by updateImageCacheProgress/updateCursor and not hidden by its clear (the cache "All" repaint clears then draws every tick). Hiding a row collapses it entirely, so the container fits only the live rows. A row's effective visibility is active && enabled: update functions set "active", and MW::setCacheProgressEnabled(G::showCacheProgress) calls setRowEnabled() on the ImageCache and MetaRead rows (FocusStack is not gated).
- Progress manages its own container visibility (updateContainerVisibility, called from relayout): shown whenever a row is visible, hidden when none are. Hosts must never call progress->setVisible() for a per-row concern, which would hide a concurrent FocusStack/RawDenoise row when cache progress is off. Two host hooks remain: setSuppressed(true) force-hides the container (a random slideshow, which does no caching), and reset() clears and hides every row when the folder is closed (MW::reset / MW::nullFiltration).
- Layout. The rows block is vertically centred (paintEvent) with topPad/botPad reserved, so a single row lines up with the other status text. setContainerWidth() sizes the bars to the available status-bar width (MW::updateProgressBarWidth via availableSpaceForProgressBar), setTextFontSize() is the separate text size, setBackgroundColor() matches the status bar.
- Height. The container grows to fit the visible rows and Progress::sizeHint() reports it, so the status bar grows. heightChanged() is also connected in MW to set the status-bar minimum height; because QStatusBar centres its widgets and reserves its own vertical margin, the handler requests a few extra pixels (h + overhead), or the reserved padding is squeezed out when Progress fills the bar. MW floors the status-bar height at its pre-Progress height (MW::statusBarBaseHeight), so collapsing rows never clips the other status text.
- clicked() opens the Caching preferences.

G::showCacheProgress gates both ImageCache and MetaRead progress: when false, progress is neither calculated nor displayed (ImageCache::updateStatus forces InfoOnly, MetaRead::dispatch skips its progress emit, and the rows are disabled). It is set by Preferences > Caching > "Hide caching progress", persisted as "showCacheProgress", default true.

### 5.3 Icon Caching

Each icon is a 256 px long-side image (\~178 KB as an ARGB QPixmap), held in the path-keyed IconStore and served through DataModel::data(Qt::DecorationRole) (see [4.5.4 IconStore](#454-iconstore)). How many are held is a balance between performance and memory, governed by dm->iconChunkSize, decided per folder in DataModel::resolveIconChunkSize (called from endLoad). The loading and eviction machinery (setIconRange, MetaRead::needToRead, clearIconsOutsideChunkRange) keys off iconChunkSize &lt; rowCount().

#### 5.3.1 Brute Force (G::useJitIconCache == false, the Default)

Cache an icon for every row, but only if they fit: iconChunkSize = min(rows, max(iconBudgetCount(), iconChunkFloor()), maxIconChunkOrAll()). A folder small enough to fit behaves exactly as "cache everything"; a 43,000-image scope gets a bounded sliding window (see [17.10 What Limits a Large Scope](#1710-what-limits-a-large-scope)). G::maxIconChunk is Preferences > "Thumbnails held in memory". The G::memoryOverrunFlag bail in DataModel::setIcon1 remains the crash backstop.

#### 5.3.2 Just in Time (G::useJitIconCache == true)

Preferences > "Cache thumbs just in time": HOLD THE SCREENS AROUND THE ONE BEING LOOKED AT, and nothing else. iconChunkFloor() is the previous, current and next screens (3x the visible page, minimum 256), which is what a person scrolling needs in hand.

It used to size the window from the memory BUDGET, which on a machine with memory to spare is most of the model, so turning JIT on changed almost nothing and the window stayed at the thumbnail ceiling (2,000 rows for a 40-row page). Every scroll asked the loader for up to 2,000 thumbnails to show 40, and the GUI thread absorbed them as queued icon events ("icons set = 4792" in one second, inside a 1,832 ms stall). The chunk is a memory bound; under this option it stops being the read-ahead list.

- Layer 1, the budget: iconBudgetCount() is how many icons fit free memory after a safety reserve and the image cache's own remaining claim (G::imageCacheHeadroomMB, published by ImageCache::memChk), times G::jitIconCacheMemFraction. It still bounds brute force.
- The floor OVERRIDES the budget. If the image cache has claimed most of memory and the budget would fall below 3x the visible icons, the floor wins and the thumbnails take the memory they need; the image cache self-throttles, because its ceiling is derived from G::availableMemoryMB, which drops as the thumbnails are held. MW::updateIconRange re-applies the floor whenever the visible count changes (e.g. switching to the denser Grid view).
- Layer 2, the measured footprint: DataModel::setIcon1 still accumulates the true per-icon size (avgIconMB and the diagnostics read it), but it is no longer acted on. It existed to GROW a JIT window once the footprint proved it would fit, and growing the window back toward the budget is exactly the cost the option exists to avoid.
- Layer 3, the pressure valve (applyIconCachePressure): a 1 s GUI-thread timer watches memory pressure (DataModel::memoryPressureLevel, from G::availableMemoryMB). On warn it halves the window; on critical it clamps to the visible page and evicts. It never grows. A 60 s cooldown plus a 2 GB available-memory high-water mark (hysteresis) gate when the latch releases, so the cache cannot thrash between shrink and re-grow. Releasing does not re-grow; the next folder load re-decides. Only active under JIT.

#### 5.3.3 The Visible Count

Independent of the mode, MW::updateIconRange grows iconChunkSize to at least the number of visible icons when more are visible (thumbView, gridView or tableView) than the current chunk, e.g. after an app or thumbnail resize. When iconChunkSize changes or there is a scroll event, MetaRead is re-dispatched to update the icons.

The visible count is the LARGEST SINGLE VIEW'S PAGE, never a span that reaches the end of the model (2026-09-24). Two routes turned it into the whole library in a 148,567-row catalog, and since brute-force growth is grow-only, one bad measurement was permanent: the chunk went 10,000 -> 148,206 and MetaRead loaded 84,000+ thumbnails.

1. IconView::updateVisible fell back to rowCount-1 whenever the bottom-right probe found no cell, which also happens mid-list when the probe lands in the spacing between cells, as it often does after a rejustify ("visible = 361 - 148566"). The fallback is now one page past the first visible cell, clamped to the last row, which is also right at the real end of the list.
2. MW::updateIconRange sized the chunk from the UNION of the visible views, and the filmstrip and the table scroll independently until the sync lands ("visible = 3083 - 72935": two 60-row pages 70,000 rows apart). dm->visibleIcons is now the largest single view's page; dm->firstVisibleIcon/lastVisibleIcon remain the union, which is what the emit gate wants.

### 5.4 Load Responsiveness

The GUI-thread cost of a folder load is dominated not by decoding but by the flood of model signals each row change emits, every one of which runs the proxy plus all the views' handlers synchronously. On a \~9,000-image recursive tree this was \~30 s of GUI-thread time, starving keys and mouse for seconds. Three measures cut it to near zero:

1. Batch per-row writes (always on). DataModel::setIcon1, setValDm and the other write paths wrap their setData calls in a QSignalBlocker and emit ONE dataChanged.
2. Notify only visible rows, coalesced (G::useVisibleOnlyIconEmit, default true). See [4.8.1 Visible Rows Only, Coalesced](#481-visible-rows-only-coalesced).
3. Batch the folder insert (G::useBatchedFolderInsert, default TRUE). DataModel::addFolder adds a folder's rows with a single setRowCount (one rowsInserted, one view relayout) and fills the cells with signals blocked plus one dataChanged for the range, instead of one rowsInserted + \~20 dataChanged per file. It cut the Phase 1 insert \~34%.

The batched insert once reversed the order (Z-A): while a batched load runs, DataModel::scheduleProcessing now turns the proxy's dynamic sort/filter OFF (sf->setDynamicSortFilter(false)), so the one wide dataChanged per folder does not re-sort the inserted block; inserted rows map in source (lessThan / name) order, and DataModel::restoreProxySortAfterLoad re-enables dynamic sort in one pass when the load finishes or aborts (every processNextBatch exit path).

These help any icon-cache mode. Set the flags false to restore the per-signal behaviour.

### 5.5 Testing Icon Caching

Flags (Main/global.cpp), flipped at runtime via the debugger or a temporary code change:

```
G::useJitIconCache           false = brute force (bounded); true = JIT (3 screens)
G::jitIconCacheMemFraction   share of the free-memory remainder budgeted (0.5)
G::iconPressureTestLevel     forces the Layer 3 pressure level (values below)
G::useVisibleOnlyIconEmit    true = per-row writes notify visible rows only
G::useBatchedFolderInsert    true = one rowsInserted + one dataChanged per folder
G::throttleFolderLoadMsg     true = addFolder's "Searching for images..." message is
                             throttled to ~50 ms instead of once per folder (removes
                             ~1.3 s of synchronous repaints on a 1,333-folder load)
G::isPerfProbe               true = concise "[PERF]" lines (see [[Probe Switches]])
```

Help > Diagnostics > DataModel report shows the live state: iconChunkSize, icon cache mode (JIT window / brute force), icon loaded (row ranges), icon avg footprint (measured vs worst-case), icon budget (icons), icon chunk floor (3x visible), imageCacheHeadroomMB, memoryPressureLevel, iconCachePressureLatched.

- Brute force: set G::useJitIconCache = false and load any folder small enough to fit. "icon loaded" spans every row and "icon cache mode" = brute force (full).
- JIT: set G::useJitIconCache = true. iconChunkSize is the 3-screen floor and the loaded rows follow the scroll.
- Layer 3, with the test override so the machine need not be starved:

```
  G::iconPressureTestLevel values:
    -1  use the real signal (availableMemoryMB)
     0  normal AND memory recovered      -> latch releases after the 60 s cooldown
     1  warn                             -> window halved, latched
     2  critical                         -> window clamped to the visible page, latched
     3  normal BUT memory not recovered  -> reaches the release branch, held by high-water
```

```
Suggested sequence (JIT on, a windowed folder loaded):
```

```
  1. = 2   critical: iconChunkSize drops to the visible page, icons evicted, latched.
  2. = 3   pressure "cleared" but not recovered: after 60 s, still latched.
  3. = 0   recovered: the latch releases on the next 1 s tick.
  4. = -1  restore the real signal.
```

```
Confirm each transition in the DataModel diagnostics and the applyIconCachePressure log lines.
```

### 5.6 Icon Loading Rules

These are the invariants the icon machinery depends on. Each was learned from a defect (see [5.10.5 Why a Catalog Scope Would Not Scroll (Nine Defects, One Policy, and Where It Ends)](#5105-why-a-catalog-scope-would-not-scroll-nine-defects-one-policy-and-where-it-ends)).

- The icon chunk MUST contain the visible window. A row outside the chunk needs no repaint notification because it cannot be on screen, and a row on screen is never a candidate for eviction. MW::updateIconRange centres the chunk on the MID-VISIBLE row whenever a visible range has been established, and falls back to the selection only when it has not (folder load, view switch, before layout). Any new caller of setIconRange must pass a row the user is actually looking at.
- Read-ahead is not retention. "Cache thumbs just in time" sets the read-ahead DISTANCE (the chunk); "Thumbnails held in memory" sets the retention BOUND. Eviction keeps the chunk grown symmetrically to the retention size (with a 256 window and a 2,000 ceiling, \~870 rows either side of what is being fetched), so an icon must fall that far behind before it is dropped. needToRead fetches only within the chunk and iconChunkMissing asks only about the chunk; retention is purely an eviction concern. With the ceiling on "No limit" nothing is evicted.
- needToRead decides first and marks second. Marking a row in rowsReading (the worker-local "a Reader has this one" set) before deciding whether it needs reading poisons it: only a returning Reader or an instance change clears the mark, and a row no Reader was dispatched for gets neither. Harmless on a folder (every row arrives MetaNotAttempted, so every row touched IS dispatched), fatal on a catalog scope (rows arrive MetaLoaded, so outside the chunk nothing is needed and every row the walk passed was poisoned).
- Clearing a loaded icon does not make MetaRead re-read it. needToRead short-circuits on readSuccessThisCycle (rows a Reader has already returned). Anything that discards loaded icons from outside the loader must call MetaRead::invalidateLoadedIcons (queued, before the setStartRow that should act on it), as MW::setPreviewSource, devPreviewUpdated and refreshStaleRows do. setStartRow re-arms the VISIBLE rows on every call in both modes, and the JIT and redo re-arm loops include VIDEO rows: a failed video decode sets IconLoaded = true (DataModel::clearVideoReadingFlag), so it is not retried, and a video still decoding is held by videoRowsReading, which needToRead tests first, so no second QMediaPlayer starts on the same file.
- G::iconChunkLoaded is maintained incrementally. iconChunkMissing is the number of rows in the current range still owing an icon, recounted exactly by setIconRange (every scroll event, so drift cannot outlive one event) and decremented as icons land. countIconChunkMissing must keep the same video / not-Present exemptions as isAllIconChunkLoaded, or the loader would redo forever chasing a row nobody expects an icon from. (A model-wide O(1) gate in front of a chunk-local requirement never closed once the model outgrew the chunk.)
- A dispatch cycle judges its OWN range. MetaRead::dispatch counts what is missing in the range captured when setStartRow ran, not G::iconChunkLoaded (which describes the range right now). A cycle whose range has moved finishes rather than redoing; redo is for a read that failed in the range it was asked about, and it is bounded by progress (see [17.19.5 The Redo Loop That Could Never Finish](#17195-the-redo-loop-that-could-never-finish)).
- Eviction walks the difference. clearIconsOutsideChunkRange walks only the rows the chunk has just slid off (the difference between the previous sweep's range and this one), the OLD window when the range jumps clear of it, and a full sweep every 64 sweeps regardless, because a reader can deliver an icon for a row that was in range when dispatched and out of range when it lands. Its writes are blocked and routed through iconRowVisible / scheduleVisibleEmit like every other per-row write. A proxy layoutChanged resets the delta (lastEvictStart/End).
- Reader backpressure pairs exactly. queuedReaderEvents is incremented by Reader before it emits and decremented only in addMetadataForItemFromReader, the one entry point where that pairing is true. (The decrement once lived inside addMetadataForItem, which a dozen non-Reader callers also reach, so the catalog fill drove it to minus the row count and wedged the backpressure valve open.) MetaRead::dispatch consults it (kQueueCap), and MW::allReaderEventsDrained uses it to decide the model is up to date.

### 5.7 Memory Governor (Process Footprint, Decode Concurrency)

Winnow bounds its resident process footprint so a large folder cannot run the machine out of memory. There are three consumers of memory and three cooperating governors. The ImageCache is usually NOT the biggest consumer: with Decode Raw on, in-flight raw decoders are.

#### 5.7.1 The Three Consumers

- ImageCache (Cache/cachedata.h imCache): the decoded 8-bit display QImages, W\*H\*4 bytes each, byte-accounted by icd->sizeMB() and bounded by the cache ceiling.
- WorkingImageCache (Develop/workingimagecache.h): a SEPARATE, byte-budgeted LRU of the scene-linear float WorkingImage (W\*H\*3 floats, 3x the QImage), kept so a Develop slider re-render skips the demosaic. Default budget 768 MB (kDefaultMaxBytes; setMaxBytes() is not called). It is NOT counted by icd->sizeMB().
- In-flight decoders: each of decoderCount (= QThread::idealThreadCount) decoder threads transiently holds its working buffers. For an embedded-JPG or ordinary JPEG/HEIC decode that is \~one QImage. For a FULL-SENSOR RAW decode (UnpackCfa -> Demosaic -> RawColor) it is the float WorkingImage plus demosaic scratch, about 8x the cached QImage. The CACHED result is identical for a raw and a same-resolution JPEG, but the raw DECODE working set is \~8x, multiplied across all decoder threads.

With Decode Raw off (G::useRaw == false) a raw file is shown from its EMBEDDED JPG preview (ImageDecoder gates the sensor path on G::useRaw): one libjpeg pass, \~QImage-sized. None of the raw-specific governing engages, and that path runs at full decoder concurrency. Raw-off performance and stability are the priority and are deliberately left untouched.

#### 5.7.2 Governor 1: Raw Decode Concurrency Cap

The primary control (Cache/imagecache.cpp). N raw decodes at \~8x-QImage each can exceed the memory cap while imCache is nearly empty, so the number of CONCURRENT full-sensor raw decodes is bounded:

```
  rawDecodeLimit = clamp( (memoryAbortMB * 0.50) / (decodedQImageMB * 8), 1, decoderCount )
```

- Gated at decodeNextImage, the single choke point reached from both launchDecoders and fillCache: if the row willUseSensorDecode() and activeRawDecodes >= rawDecodeLimit, the decoder is parked (cycling[id] = false) instead of starting another decode. A finishing sensor decode decrements the counter in fillCache and frees a slot; the other decoders keep the pipeline full, so throughput holds at the limit.
- willUseSensorDecode() is false for JPEG/HEIC and the Decode-Raw-off embedded path, so those are never gated.
- RawFormat::HasSensorDecoder(ext) is the cheap test (a hash lookup, no decoder constructed). It and RawFormat::Create() both derive from one extension -> decoder-factory table, rawFactories() in ImageFormats/Raw/rawformat.cpp, so "which extensions have a sensor decoder" lives in exactly one place. Adding a format's sensor decoder is a one-line change there.
- Extension membership over-approximates (a compressed ARW matches but its Decode() falls back to the embedded JPG). That is the safe direction for a memory guard: the first decode must assume the heavy path, and such fallbacks decode cheaply anyway.
- decoderIsRaw[id] marks a decoder on the sensor path so the decrement fires exactly once per decode; both are reset per folder in initialize(). On a big-RAM machine the larger memoryAbortMB opens the limit back toward full concurrency.

#### 5.7.3 Governor 2: Image Cache Ceiling Clamp

In ImageCache::memChk, maxMBCeiling (the cache's growth target) is derived from availableMemoryMB, then clamped so cache budget + measured non-cache footprint + a per-decoder reserve stays under memoryAbortMB. The non-cache footprint is measured live, so it already includes in-flight decoders, and the cache automatically plans fewer images while raw decodes are consuming memory.

#### 5.7.4 Governor 3: Memory Watchdog

MW::memoryWatchdogTick, a 50 ms GUI-thread probe, is a graduated backstop. cap = G::memoryAbortMB (computeMemoryAbortMB scales it to host RAM, e.g. \~18.4 GB on 24 GB):

- footprint >= cap: engage the ImageCache throttle. setMemoryThrottled(true) parks decoders at decodeNextImage, and memoryPause() (queued to the cache thread) shrinks and trims imCache. No dialog.
- footprint &lt;= 0.88 \* cap: release the throttle; memoryResume() relaunches decoders.
- footprint >= cap + max(2 GB, cap/10): a runaway the throttle could not contain. Fall back to the hard onMemoryOverrun abort dialog (prevents an OS OOM). With the concurrency cap in place the footprint should not approach the cap during raw traversal, so this exists for the pathological case.

#### 5.7.5 Diagnostics and Tunables

ImageCache::diagnostics() prints a "Memory Footprint / Raw Decode" block (process footprint, imCache MB/count, WorkingImageCache MB/count/budget, G::useRaw, decoderCount, active/peak raw decodes, the computed limit and per-decode estimate) and a "Memory Pressure Warnings" ring buffer of timestamped PAUSE / RESUME / CRITICAL events. A large footprint with a small imCache and a WorkingImageCache at \~budget confirms the memory is in the concurrent raw decoders, which the concurrency cap bounds.

Tunables: rawDecodeLimit()'s 0.50 budget fraction and x8 per-decode factor (Cache/imagecache.cpp); the watchdog's 0.88 resume hysteresis and critical headroom (MW::memoryWatchdogTick); computeMemoryAbortMB() (Main/global.cpp) for the host-scaled cap.

### 5.8 Thumbnails in the Index (ThumbCache)

Scrolling a catalog cannot open a file per row. Winnow's thumbnails come from an embedded preview inside the image, so producing one means opening the file, walking to the preview's segment and decoding it: affordable for a folder of 500, not as the scroll position of a 250,000-image library. The index's `thumb` table (added in schema 5) decodes each icon ONCE, ever, so a later scroll is a database read. ThumbCache is the interface.

The read chain is memory store -> index -> decode, and it reads as one chain because all three are keyed the same way: Datamodel/iconstore.h is path-keyed, and the table keys on cachePathKey(), the same key the image and keyword tables use, so the same file spelled with a doubled slash or a different drive-letter case is one row rather than two.

The payload is a BLOB, the opposite of what devpreview does, because of payload SIZE. A devPreview is a full-resolution JPEG of one to three megabytes, for which a file is the right container. A thumbnail is ten to thirty kilobytes, and a quarter of a million of those as files is 250,000 inodes with a per-file open dominating every read; SQLite beats the filesystem for blobs of that size, and its page cache serves a scroll from memory. The COLUMNS still mirror devpreview, so the two share one eviction and sweep policy.

Settings: "Cache thumbnails" (G::cacheThumbnails) and "Thumbnail cache size" are in Preferences > Caching with every other cache setting (2026-10-13). Moves and deletes go through Utilities/fileops.h, so a renamed file keeps its thumbnail.

#### 5.8.1 Freshness and the Sweep

Staleness is the one failure a cache must not have. An image edited by another program keeps its path, so a thumbnail returned on identity alone would be yesterday's picture for today's file. Every row stamps the source's size and mtime, and a mismatch is a MISS. A row stamped with zeros predates the stamp and is grandfathered, as DevPreviewCache does for its imported rows.

The sweep DEMOTES, never deletes, and skips entries whose volume is not mounted. An ejected card, an unplugged drive or a share that is not up looks identical to a deletion from the inside, and throwing away a whole volume's thumbnails because it was not plugged in is what makes a cache feel unreliable. A missing file is marked live = 0, which puts it first in the eviction order without destroying it, so a file restored from the trash finds its thumbnail again. The sweep pages on rowid (see [5.10.2 Thumbnail Cache Checks That Reported Success](#5102-thumbnail-cache-checks-that-reported-success)).

#### 5.8.2 Writing Thumbnails as They Load

Thumbnails are written at the PRODUCER, not at the model. Reader::readIcon and FrameDecoder both have the decoded image in hand and are already off the GUI thread; DataModel::setIcon1 runs ON the GUI thread, where a JPEG encode and a database write per icon would land on the load path. ThumbCache::putImage is the single entry point both call, so the encode, the staleness stamp and the skip-if-present check exist once. The video case is worth more than the still: a video's icon costs an AVFoundation frame grab, so both video paths write too.

Camera thumbnails only, decided by where the pixels came from (fixed 2026-10-10). The table is keyed by path and its freshness stamp is the FILE's size and mtime, so it must only ever hold the camera's picture; a developed thumbnail stored here would outlive its recipe, because resetting a recipe changes the sidecar, never the file. Reader::readIcon used to rely on putImage's developEdited guard, and a flag that was ever wrong for the row (a stale ImageMetadata on an icon-only read, a model column not yet updated) stored the sidecar's developed thumbnail as the camera thumb. Seen on a D7200 NEF that was edited (crop + colour) and later reset: the grid kept the old crop and colour while the loupe was correct. Thumb::loadThumb now sets lastWasDevThumb when loadDevThumb answered, and readIcon never offers such an image to putImage. Schema 23 is the matching data repair: it deletes the thumb rows of every image that has develop_history (the only images that could have had a developed thumbnail), and they are re-read from the files.

One writer thread, batched transactions. Doing the work inline on each loader thread measured badly (50 mixed raw files, median of five runs, per icon):

```
  caching off                  30.1 ms
  inline, index empty          43.7 ms     +47%
  inline, index already full   34.1 ms     +15%
  queued, index empty          39.0 ms     +30%   (the encode, once per image ever)
  queued, index already full   32.2 ms     within the run-to-run spread of "off" (27.7-32.1)
```

Inline, every statement was its own transaction and several reader threads serialised on one writer, so even the WARM case (one indexed SELECT, then skip) cost 4.5 ms an icon. Queued to one writer, the remaining cold cost is the encode itself competing for CPU with the readers, paid once per image for the life of the index.

- The handoff is a queued signal, not a hand-rolled queue. The first attempt was a QThread with a QList, a QMutex and two QWaitConditions, and ThreadSanitizer complained about the shared list under real load (both accesses appeared to hold the same mutex, a report that does not lead anywhere quickly). The worker is now a QObject on its own thread, jobs arrive by queued signal, and batching happens in a list that only exists on the worker's thread, so nothing is shared and nothing needs a lock.
- flush() is a BLOCKING queued invoke, which cannot run until everything ahead of it has: no condition variable, no busy-wait.
- The backlog is bounded and drops. A queued QImage is a quarter of a megabyte, so an unbounded backlog behind a slow disk would be a memory leak. Dropping costs nothing; the next visit offers the thumbnail again.
- ThumbCache::written() counts what the writer actually encoded and stored (see [5.10.2 Thumbnail Cache Checks That Reported Success](#5102-thumbnail-cache-checks-that-reported-success)).

#### 5.8.3 Locking and the Read Path

Only shared state goes under the lock. The read path takes NO mutex for the statement:

- CacheDb hands out one connection per thread, so no two threads share a QSqlDatabase, and the file is in WAL, where a reader blocks neither a writer nor another reader. A mutex around the SELECT was hand-serialising what SQLite already provides.
- ThumbCache::mMutex guards what is genuinely shared: the writer thread's lifetime, the byte cap, and the write paths against each other (written on its declaration). The writer handle is a std::atomic published after the object is wired up (ThumbCache::writerOrStart), double-checked so the mutex is reached once per session: a hit or a put reads a pointer, not a queue.
- ThumbCache::writeBatch does its stat, its skip-if-present SELECT and its JPEG ENCODE outside the lock, keeping only the transaction inside.
- The LRU `used` stamp is not written on the read path. It orders eviction, not correctness, so it is refreshed only when more than a day old, and the refresh goes to the writer thread (ThumbWriter::takeStamp -> ThumbCache::writeStampBatch), coalesced on its own slow timer (kStampDelayMs 2000, kStampBatch 1024, ThumbWriter::flushStamps). A zero-timer would batch nothing: it fires whenever the writer's loop is idle, which with hits trickling in is after every stamp. Losing a batch at exit costs an eviction ordering nobody can perceive. `live = 1` rides along with it.
- A hit is not written back. Reader tracks whether the picture came from the cache and does not offer it to putImage.
- The caller supplies the stat when it has one. ThumbCache::getImage compares the stored row against the file's size and mtime; on a metadata+icon read the Reader has already stat'd the file (Metadata::loadImageMetadata's QFileInfo, or IndexMetadata::candidate), so Reader carries srcSize/srcMtime on the task (reset per task in Reader::read) and getImage stats only when they arrive as -1. The values are a contract in the writer's own terms (bytes; mtime in whole SECONDS), and wrong ones fail as a false miss, never a stale picture; tst_thumbcache::getImageUsesACallerSuppliedStat pins both halves.
- The icon-only read keeps its own stat. Riding on the scroll-in verification was measured and dropped: the icon read is dispatched the moment updateIconRange moves, while ScrollVerify runs 400 ms after scrolling STOPS. Believing the row's ByteSizeColumn / ModifiedColumn instead would be a real weakening: in a folder scope nothing else notices a file edited by another program mid-session, so getImage's own stat is the last check that the picture was made from the bytes on disk.

A cache hit is about 390 us of real work: 73 us stat, 52 us SELECT, 263 us JPEG decode (measured on a quiet scroll). The thumbnail cache is not a bottleneck.

Still open and unmeasured: evictLocked runs after EVERY batch, starts with a SELECT SUM(bytes) over a table of blobs, and deletes row by row outside a transaction (one WAL commit per evicted row). Testing it, and the stamp coalescing and the writer's transaction hold, needs a COLD folder with a full cache; the probes (writer hold / prep / evict, lruStamps, stampBatches) are in place.

#### 5.8.4 Reading Them Back

Reader::readIcon asks the index before it opens anything. A hit replaces opening the file, walking to its embedded preview and decoding it with one indexed read and a small JPEG decode; a miss costs one stat and one indexed lookup and falls through to exactly the code that ran before. Per icon, median of five runs:

```
  a folder with no develop edits (all 12 images cacheable)
      no cache        31.4 ms
      cold (writing)  43.2 ms
      WARM             8.3 ms      3.8x
```

```
  the 50-file mixed folder (26 of 50 cacheable)
      no cache        32.6 ms
      cold (writing)  41.2 ms
      WARM            28.5 ms
```

Cold is dearer than no cache at all, once per image for the life of the index; that is the trade the whole thing rests on.

The gate is PER IMAGE. Thumb::loadThumb does not always return the camera's thumbnail: for an image with a develop recipe, in Develop mode or with the preview source set to Developed, it returns the DEVELOPED thumbnail from the sidecar. Reading the index in that case would show the camera picture where the user asked for the edit (and writing it would poison the index). Only an EDITED image in a developed-showing mode is excluded; an UNEDITED image has no developed thumbnail at any setting, so Thumb::devThumb falls through to the camera's picture and the cache is exactly right. hasDevelopRecipe comes from ImageMetadata::developEdited, which the metadata read has already established, so the per-image test costs nothing.

- The first version gated on the MODE alone. G::previewSource DEFAULTS to Developed, so the cache was switched off entirely and every measurement came back "no change", which is what a feature that never runs looks like. Three unit cases pin the per-image gate, including that an unedited image is cacheable at the DEFAULT setting; the injected mode-only gate fails all three by name.
- In practice a heavily edited library gets less from this than an unedited one: the mixed folder has 24 develop-edited images of 50, and caches the other 26.

What comes back is indistinguishable from what the decoder produces: RGB32, scaled to no more than G::maxIconSize. A row written by an older build or under a larger icon setting is scaled down on the way out (the same guard Thumb::devThumb applies to a sidecar preview), so a changed icon-size preference cannot paint over a cell.

### 5.9 Metadata From the Index

Preferences > Library > "Read metadata from the catalog" (G::useIndexMetadata, default OFF), beside the thumbnail settings, because both answer "what does Winnow keep so it does not have to read the file again".

Reader::readMetadata asks Catalog::fetchFresh first. A hit fills ImageMetadata from the index and skips the file read (\~20 ms for a raw, almost all of it walking the file's own header); a miss falls through to the code that ran before.

Status: a row served from the catalog is byte-identical to the same row read from its file, across all four test folders, over every resident column of every row. ThreadSanitizer is clean on both the plain and the proxy-stress runs (fetchFresh is called from the Reader threads), the QAbstractItemModelTester gate is clean, and so is the recursive navigation-plus-sort-reversal stress run. It stays off by default because all of that was verified HEADLESSLY; nothing has exercised it by a person navigating, editing and ingesting, and the failure mode of a wrong row is quiet. The preference is how it gets tried.

What it is worth, on the 50-file mixed folder with the thumbnail cache warm: 32.2 ms per icon down to 25.1 ms, about 22%. On a folder whose thumbnails are NOT cached, the icon path reads the header anyway (below), so the saving is a revisit saving, narrower than the raw 20 ms suggests.

#### 5.9.1 fetchFresh and staleOf Partition the Candidates

Catalog::fetchFresh is staleOf() read the other way round. staleOf answers "what must I INDEX?" for the scanner, which then reads those files; fetchFresh answers "what need I not READ?" for the loader, which then skips them. Same stamp (source size, source mtime, sidecar mtime), same comparison, opposite consumer.

The two must partition the candidates EXACTLY. If they ever disagree in the same direction, an image is both skipped and unindexed: invisible, and PERMANENTLY so, because nothing would revisit it until its file changed. The test for that invariant varies every stamp field. It originally built three candidates (unchanged, srcSize moved, never catalogued), and an injected fetchFresh that ignored the SIDECAR stamp passed it; a fourth candidate now differs only in its sidecar mtime (the ordinary case of a keyword edited in Lightroom, which rewrites the .xmp and never touches the raw), and the injection fails naming the file and both verdicts.

- One prepared statement is reused rather than "WHERE pathkey IN (...)": a folder of 5,000 images would put 5,000 bound values into one statement, and SQLite's parameter limit is lower than that on some builds. The lookup is on the primary key, so the loop is 5,000 index seeks, which is what an IN would compile to anyway.

#### 5.9.2 The Contract It Changes: Segment Offsets on Demand

ImageCache::okToDecode gates the decoder on MetaLoaded precisely BECAUSE MetaLoaded promises the segment offsets are populated. A row filled from the index has none. So:

- ImageMetadata::fromIndex marks such a row, and DataModel::addMetadataForItem leaves the scratch columns UNWRITTEN for it. Writing zeros would be worse than nothing: the scratch store's set mask would report them written, an offset of 0 is legal, and the decoder would decode from the front of the file. Leaving them unset makes the gap detectable; it is the reason the set mask exists.
- ImageDecoder::ensureDecodeGeometry reads the header at the point of decode, on the thread about to open the file anyway. The header walk moves from every row at load time to only the rows the user opens.
- ImageDecoder::ensureIndependentGeometry is the same read for an INDEPENDENT decode: the devPreview builder, an export, focus stack, Develop's own re-decode. Those are handed a whole ImageMetadata built by DataModel::imMetadata, which copies the scratch columns, so an index-served row hands them zero offsets with no sfRow to notice the gap on. It showed as "ImageDecoder::decode failed" on every CR3 the moment the catalog was browsed, and on CR3 alone: the other raw decoders self-walk their container when RawSensorInfo is missing, while CRX falls back to the embedded preview, which is exactly what the missing offsets point at. It reads with a LOCAL Metadata (the one an independent decoder holds belongs to MW) and publishes nothing back.
- The geometry is held on the DECODER for one decode, not read back from the model, because the writes that publish it for next time are QUEUED to the GUI thread and have not landed while the decode runs. It is used by load() for the offsets and colorManage() for the ICC profile (hence a member, not a local), and reset at the top of every decode so one row's geometry can never be read for another's.
- The icon path needs the offsets too. Reader::readIcon passes the embedded thumbnail's offset and length to Thumb::presetOffset; without them, the formats that depend on those offsets fell back to the ERROR ICON (an Icon Aspect Ratio of exactly 1, because error_image256.png is square). It reads the header when the thumbnail cache has already missed, which costs nothing extra because that thread is about to open the file regardless. The geometry is used LOCALLY: publishing it with addToDatamodel doubled every field of the row's searchable text, because addMetadataForItem APPENDS to it (twenty-three rows in fifty ended with their dimensions and camera twice over).

#### 5.9.3 What the Catalog Must Store to Fill a Row

The catalog originally stored what SEARCH needs, not what DISPLAY needs. Fingerprinting index-served rows against file-read rows found the gaps, closed by:

- Schema 6: orientation (the serious one: an index-served row read 0 where the file said 1, and orientation drives rotation), exposurecomp, focusx, focusy, email, url, the seven orig\_\* columns (how an edit is reverted, and how a sidecar write decides whether anything changed), developed and devpreviewkey. One ALTER TABLE ADD COLUMN each. The migration also set every freshness stamp to -1: after the ALTERs every indexed row was INCOMPLETE while its stamp said current, so nothing would ever re-read it and orientation would stay 0 forever. It costs one re-index of whatever had been catalogued. tst_catalog::displayFieldsSurviveTheRoundTrip pins the fields through both the INSERT and the UPDATE paths (the two statements bind the same sequence and it is easy to extend one and not the other).
- Schema 7: keywordpaths (the "A|B|C" strings as the file spelled them; the flat node names are still what is searched and filtered, but a row's searchable TEXT is built from the original spelling), keywords_literal (dc:subject as the file spelled it, a THIRD keyword fact: only the literal list may ever be written back, since handing the flattened one to a row would put every ancestor into the user's own dc:subject at the next sidecar write), and shootinginfo. shootingInfo looks redundant to store and is not: Metadata::loadImageMetadata composes it only when the read SUCCEEDED, while Thumb::setImageDimensions marks a row MetaLoaded from the thumbnail path whether the read succeeded or not, so a catalogued row may legitimately carry an empty one. (The real defect is MetaLoaded meaning two things depending on which path set it.) Its spelling matters too: "1/80 sec at f/5.6", with " sec", because it is shown verbatim.
- captured is SECONDS SINCE EPOCH. fetchFresh had read it with QVariant::toDateTime, which on an integer yields a date parsed from its digits: an A7R2 shot in September 2016 came back as April 2017. It reads fromSecsSinceEpoch now.

#### 5.9.4 Bugs the Fingerprint Found in the Loader

- Width and Height were the EMBEDDED PREVIEW's size. The catalog held 160 where the file said 6016, because Thumb::setImageDimensions wrote the same decoded size to both G::WidthColumn (how big the IMAGE is: what the table shows, what MPix, Dimensions and Aspect Ratio derive from, what gets catalogued) and G::WidthOrigPreviewColumn (how big the embedded preview is, which the image cache budgets memory from). That is right for paths that decode the whole file and wrong for ones that decode the preview, and HEIC takes the second kind on both platforms (Heic::decodeThumbnail on Windows, macImageIOThumbnail on macOS), so whichever of the metadata read and the thumbnail decode landed last decided what the row said. setImageDimensions now takes the two sizes SEPARATELY, and an invalid fullSize means "I only decoded the preview", in which case the image dimensions are left alone. If the metadata read failed they stay 0, which is honest; a plausible wrong number is worse than a missing one, because nothing downstream can tell. Verified on the 50-file folder: no width at or below G::maxIconSize on any row, and an A7R2 reads 8000 wide with a 1616-wide preview.
- QImageReader::size() is not reliably the full image. On macOS a raw goes through the ImageIO plugin, which reports the dimensions of whatever representation it decoded (for a NEF, the 160 px embedded preview), and Thumb::loadFromEntireFile passed it on as the image's size. loadFromEntireFile now prefers the metadata read's dimensions; QImageReader is the fallback for formats with no metadata read of their own.

Note that several early A/B runs were taken against stale catalog data written before these fixes, because the catalog capture itself was silently not running headlessly (see [17.19.2 The Catalog Capture Was Silently Not Running](#17192-the-catalog-capture-was-silently-not-running)). Once it ran, the divergence collapsed from eight columns to three, and then to zero.

### 5.10 Investigations and Fixes

#### 5.10.1 What Phase 2 Actually Costs (Icons, Not the Metadata Read)

"A metadata read is \~20 ms for a raw, and almost all of it is walking the file's own header" was the sentence the index-metadata path was built on, and it made "MetaRead should stop reading rows the index can answer" look like the next thing worth doing. Measured, it is not true.

1,048 Sony ARW files (each with an .xmp sidecar), Phase 2 wall time from folderChanged to MetaRead::done, warm page cache, WINNOW_PERF_PROBE=1:

```
  icon chunk 10,000 (every row), index metadata OFF      22,360 ms
  icon chunk 10,000 (every row), index metadata ON       20,888 ms   (idxHit 1,045, idxMiss 0)
  icon chunk 50,     index metadata OFF   679, 1,019, 950 ms
  icon chunk 50,     index metadata ON  1,105, 852, 1,076 ms   (idxHit ~1,042, idxMiss 0)
```

- Icons are \~95% of Phase 2. Capping the icon chunk at 50 takes the same folder from 20.9 s to about 1 s, with the metadata for all 1,048 rows still read in both. A thumbnail cost about 20 ms; the metadata read about 1 ms. The whole phase is the icon window, the same conclusion the 43,000-image measurement reached about MEMORY, arrived at independently for TIME.
- The index makes no measurable difference to the metadata read. The first chunk-50 pair looked like a 60% LOSS for the index (1,105 against 679 ms), and repeating it did not reproduce: three runs each give 679-1,019 ms without and 852-1,105 ms with, so the spread within each setting is as large as the gap between them. \~1 ms a row either way, with the catalog answering every row (idxMiss 0; those counters exist because "the index made no difference" and "the index was never consulted" are opposite conclusions an A/B cannot otherwise tell apart). Catalog::fetchFresh does one SQLite seek plus a sidecar stat per row, about what the header walk it replaces costs. A single A/B pair at this scale is a coin toss.
- Caveats: a warm page cache, one folder, one camera, one machine. A cold cache slows both paths, and the icon read (far more bytes) more, so the ratio is if anything conservative. The revisit saving in [5.9 Metadata From the Index](#59-metadata-from-the-index) is a different measurement of a different thing and still stands.

The consequence is a decision. "MetaRead becomes the gap-filler, not the primary loader" was aimed at \~5% of the load, and the mechanism it would be built on does not make even that part faster; the \~50-call-site change to what G::allMetadataAttempted MEANS existed only to serve it. Both were CLOSED on this measurement, not deferred. It was the third time on this work that a load-pipeline assumption failed measurement (see also the centralMsg repaint and "the keywords are most of the saving"), which is the argument for probe knobs rather than the next redesign.

What replaced them: make the ICON cheaper, or load fewer of them. Decomposing the first found a 36x defect in the first run (see [5.10.6 A Cache Hit Was Costing a Commit (the LRU Stamp, and the Stat, on the Read Path)](#5106-a-cache-hit-was-costing-a-commit-the-lru-stamp-and-the-stat-on-the-read-path)): on a folder whose thumbnails are cached, that 20 ms was lock wait, not decode. The second already has its control (G::maxIconChunk binds and is a preference); what is unsettled is whether the brute-force chunk should still be the DEFAULT, given that the chunk size is the single biggest lever on load time.

#### 5.10.2 Thumbnail Cache Checks That Reported Success

Each was the kind of bug that reports success.

- The sweep swept nothing. It paged with the pathkey as its cursor, and a default-constructed QString is NULL to SQLite: `pathkey > NULL` is NULL rather than true, so the first page came back empty and the pass reported a clean sweep of a table full of dead rows. It pages on rowid now: an integer that starts usefully at 0, is the physical order, and is what DevPreviewCache's sweep already used.
- An assertion that passed without testing anything. The eviction case asked contains() whether an evicted row was gone, passing a stamp of 0,0; but contains() applies the staleness check, so it returns false for a row written with a real stamp whether that row exists or not. It asks the table directly now.
- A test that could not see the thing it tested. The skip-if-present check was verified by asserting that a second putImage of an unchanged file left the row count and total bytes alone, and deleting the skip did not fail it, because re-encoding an unchanged image produces byte-identical output. ThumbCache::written() now counts what the writer actually encoded and stored, and re-injecting the missing skip fails by name.

#### 5.10.3 A Full-Sensor JPEG Encode on the GUI Thread (the Pause Every 35 Images)

The report was "a short pause approximately every 35 images" when holding the right arrow through a card, with the image cache still showing images cached ahead. It was not the navigation, not the cache, and not every 35 images.

What the measurement said, in order:

1. The ingest probe's gap column put \~283 ms outside MW::fileSelectionChange, which never exceeded 13 ms.
2. The periodicity lines gave 1,542 ms between long gaps while navigating, and the stalls CONTINUED at 1,410 ms for fifteen seconds after the user stopped, with the selection count frozen: a timer, not a row count.
3. The event hog named MW(MW)/MetaCall and stopped there.
4. `sample` finished it in six seconds (at a 20% duty cycle the stack dominates the main thread):

```
MW::devPreviewBuildNext()::$_0 -> MW::devPreviewStore -> QImage::save -> jpeg_write_scanlines   832 of 852 samples
```

MW::devPreviewStore ran the scale and the JPEG encode on the GUI thread. With "Build developed previews in background" on, MW::queueBackgroundDevPreviewBuild queues every raw in the folder (3,404 on that card), and the loop renders one OFF the GUI thread, then handed the full-resolution QImage back to the GUI thread to be encoded. devPreviewMaxEdge defaults to kDevPreviewSizeFull (no cap), so that was a full-sensor JPEG at quality 90: 283 ms on a 60 MP ARW, once every \~1.4 s, for as long as the folder stayed open. Leaving the folder abandons the build (MW::stop -> cancelDevPreviewBuild), so it took an ingest session, sitting in one folder for an hour, to feel it.

The fix: both steps are pixels in, bytes out, touching no widget and no model, so both moved to a pool thread (QtConcurrent::run + QFutureWatcher) with the writes resuming on the GUI thread. What stays on the GUI thread: reading the recipe (developBlobFor reads the Develop dock), the sidecar and cache writes, and devPreviewUpdated. Two structural consequences:

- The key is checked twice. It was already re-derived after the render (a render takes seconds and the user may have edited the image meanwhile), and the encode adds a few hundred milliseconds more of the same window.
- The build advances from one place. devPreviewStore returns long before the step is finished, so the counters can no longer be bumped at the bottom of the render callback, which would start the next render while this one was still encoding. Every path out of devPreviewStore, including its early returns, calls devPreviewBuildStepDone exactly once.

Measured: WINNOW_SELFTEST_DEVPREVIEWS=1 turns the preference on for a headless run, so the same 50 s pass over the same card ran against both versions. Stall end times, in ms:

```
before   486 1243 1642 2004 2228 4032 4189 4517 | 9130 14227 19314 24403 29487 34573 39662 44753 49839
after    483 1347 1722 2067 2282 4067 4223 4666 |
```

Left of the bar is the folder load, identical. Right of it is the periodic encode: nine stalls at a flat \~5,086 ms (a headless run has a cold cache and no rendered image to reuse), and none after the move. Preview throughput is unchanged (16 previews written in the before run's tail, 18 in the after run's), the check that matters second, because a stall removed by not doing the work is not a fix.

#### 5.10.4 Two Guards That Did Not Guard (the Unlocked Read, and the bool Decoder Id)

Both found by reading the ingest path, on the "loupe does not show the selected image" complaint, and neither visible in a snapshot.

- contains() then value() is two locks with a gap. ImageView::loadImage asked icd->contains(fPath) (which locks) and then read icd->imCache.value(fPath) with no lock, while the ImageCache thread trims the same hash. Losing that race returned a default-constructed QImage, set as the pixmap with isLoaded = TRUE: a BLANK LOUPE REPORTED AS A SUCCESSFUL LOAD, and nothing to repair it, because refreshViewsOnCacheChange only fires on a cache CHANGE. It was also a data race against a rehash. ImageCacheData::get() now does the test and the fetch under one lock and returns false when the key is absent; the three callers (ImageView::loadImage, Stack::doMean, EmbelExport::loadImage) treat a null image as a miss and take their normal fallback. A null image can be in the cache legitimately (ImageCache::nullInImCache exists to find and re-queue them), so the null test is needed whether or not a trim raced.
- A decoder id declared as bool. ImageCache::instanceClash(bool id) was called with an int decoder index, so every id above 1 collapsed to 1, and okToCache tested DECODER 1's instance instead of the returning decoder's. With decoderCount = QThread::idealThreadCount, most of the pool checked the wrong thread: a stale decode could be accepted and a current one refused, at random. Now int and bounds-checked; an out-of-range id answers "clash", which only ever refuses an image.

#### 5.10.5 Why a Catalog Scope Would Not Scroll (Nine Defects, One Policy, and Where It Ends)

The report: "I cannot scroll through all the thumbnails; they fail to show, or I get the beachball", and changing the thumbnails-held-in-memory preference in either direction did not help. The defects were found with --perfprobe runs, not by reading the code; the reading had predicted isAllIconChunkLoaded, which measured 0-8 ms and was not a problem. The rules they produced are [5.6 Icon Loading Rules](#56-icon-loading-rules).

1. The beachball: evicting an icon cost 5.3 ms. clearIconsOutsideChunkRange wrote two cells per evicted row (the decoration and IconLoaded) through plain sf->setData, each emitting its own dataChanged: the one path in the icon machinery that never adopted the visible-only, coalesced notification. Each dataChanged rebuilt the Cocoa accessibility table (\~27 ms at 43,000 rows), so a sweep evicting 1,820 icons emitted 3,640 of them:

```
  [PERF] scroll 17.6 s  src = MW::gridHasScrolled
           chunk= 2000  range= 0 - 2000  sfRows= 42956  visible= 5800 - 5847  iconsLoaded= 73
           scan  calls= 2  rows= 4002  ms= 0.0
           evict calls= 1  cleared= 1820  ms= 9650.4
  [PERF] GUI STALL 17624 ms
```

```
 A row outside the chunk is off-screen by definition, so the notification had no one to tell. The same walk evicting nothing takes under a millisecond: the O(rows) sweep was never the problem.
```
2. The missing thumbnails: the chunk followed the SELECTION, not the scroll. MW::updateIconRange centred the chunk on dm->currentSfRow, and scrolling does not change the selection: chunk 0-2000 with the user looking at rows 5,800-5,847. Icons for the visible rows were evicted as fast as the loader read them (iconsLoaded 1,820 -> 73 -> 0 with the view still). It survived because the three scroll handlers call updateChange immediately afterwards, which re-centres on the mid-visible row, so on the paths anyone tests by hand the wrong range lasted microseconds; IconView::resizeEvent and rejustify call updateIconRange and nothing else, and eviction is QUEUED from the metaReadThread, so it could land inside the gap on the ordinary path too.
3. Thumbnails that would not come back: rows marked in flight for a read that was never dispatched (needToRead marked before deciding). With 1 and 2 fixed, the probe read iconsLoaded = 49 in a 2,000-row chunk with the view still.
4. G::iconChunkLoaded was recomputed from scratch on every icon. Its O(1) gate ("the chunk cannot be complete until iconLoadedCount reaches span - videos - unloadable") was MODEL-wide while the requirement is CHUNK-local, so once the model outgrew the chunk the gate never closed and every icon write ran the full walk: "scan calls = 1247 rows = 2495247 ms = 306.8" for one second of scrolling.
5. A zero timer scheduled the repaint behind the flood that caused it. With the icons in the model within milliseconds of the scroll (3,628 stored in a second, 514 redundant), the pages still took one to two seconds to appear: what was late was the NOTIFICATION. scheduleVisibleEmit's QTimer::singleShot(0) fires only when the queue is empty, and the queue was the 2,000-row chunk's icon events. It is a 20 ms timer now. Every counter had said the system was healthy because every counter measured WORK DONE; none measured the gap between "the thumbnail exists" and "the user can see it", the only quantity the complaint was about. That gap is now worstWait on the scroll line, and it fell from 3,258 ms to 38-97 ms.
6. readerQueue = -42956, exactly minus the row count: the backpressure counter's decrement lived in addMetadataForItem, which the catalog fill and a dozen other non-Reader callers reach. It now lives in addMetadataForItemFromReader.
7. The redo storm was a range mismatch: dispatch judged its cycle by G::iconChunkLoaded, which describes the CURRENT range, so a finished cycle redid up to redoMax and reported REDO MAXED OUT with noIcon = 0, dozens of times per scroll. It now counts what is missing in its own range.
8. Then the sweep itself became the top cost: "evict calls = 222 walked = 9.1M cleared = 384 ms = 949.4" in one second, 222 walks of the whole model. It now walks the difference, with a periodic full sweep.
9. The redo could not fix what it was retrying: every row a redo retries is in readSuccessThisCycle by definition, so redo was refused for exactly those rows, five times per arm. Redo now re-arms as setStartRow does. And video rows are re-armed too (2026-10-01): the WFPROBE trace showed a re-sort clear 21 video icons and only 4 come back.

The policy, not a defect: the chunk was being used as the read-ahead list. With all of the above fixed, "icons set = 4792" in one second, inside a 1,832 ms stall, to show forty rows: nothing wasted, the work item simply forty times bigger than the question. "Cache thumbs just in time" now means the previous, current and next screens (see [5.3.2 Just in Time (G::useJitIconCache == true)](#532-just-in-time-gusejiticoncache--true)). Layer 2's refineIconChunkSize was DELETED rather than disabled, because growing a JIT window back toward the memory budget is now exactly wrong, and the window follows the visible page in BOTH directions (the chunk used to be grow-only, so one glance at a dense grid left it oversized for the session). It is off by default: brute force stays right for folders, and this is the answer for a catalog scope. Its cost is that scrolling back re-reads, cheap with "Cache thumbnails" on.

That exposed read-ahead vs retention: with a 256 window the probe showed "icons set = 2222 ... cleared = 2222" second after second, every icon read dropped again almost at once, because eviction used the chunk to decide what may be kept. Eviction now keeps the chunk grown to the retention size. In the same pass, a jump that lands clear of the previous window sweeps the OLD window rather than the whole model.

A last note on redo, because the symptom is distinctive: REDO MAXED OUT reporting noIcon = exactly the visible page size, over and over, during an ordinary scroll. Those rows entered the icon range WHILE the cycle was running; a setStartRow for the new range is already queued and will read them. A cycle whose range has moved now finishes.

Where it ended: every Winnow-side figure on the scroll line is single-digit milliseconds per second of scrolling (scan 0.0, evict 0.0, setIcon1 2.4, the dataChanged emissions 65.6: about 68 ms of a 1,100 ms window). A residual stutter remained, 94% of it outside everything instrumented, so the next step was a SAMPLED PROFILE (`sample Winnow 5`) rather than a tenth counter; two bespoke-probe hypotheses had been wrong in a row, the signal to stop instrumenting what you suspect and go and look.

The profile named painting. Of \~1,160 active main-thread samples (1,609 of 2,770 were idle in mach_msg), \~362 were QWidgetRepaintManager::sync -> paintAndFlush, a third of active time. The chain descends drawWidget -> paintSiblingsRecursive four levels (202, 198, 161, 122, 104, 100) before reaching QListView::paintEvent at 97, so roughly half the paint is the icon view's own cells and half sibling widgets painting alongside it. The largest leaf in the cell paint is IconViewDelegate::paint -> QPaintEngineEx::drawRoundedRect at 28 samples: an antialiased rounded rect for the frame on EVERY cell, plus the number badge, the pick/ingest/reject border, the selection and the current index: up to five per cell, \~48 cells, per repaint, per visible view. Deliberately not fixed here: removing drawRoundedRect altogether would recover \~2.4% of active time, a win on the biggest named leaf and still not a cure. That is painting, a different subsystem (which sibling widgets repaint per scroll event, whether the viewports should be opaque, whether the three-view scroll sync forces redundant repaints), and it is still OPEN. The scroll probe stays in the tree so that work starts from measurements.

The common thread: each defect was a piece of the icon machinery written when a row meant "a file we are about to open", meeting a row that arrives already knowing everything except its picture. For an index-hydrated row, metadata-attempted no longer implies read-attempted.

#### 5.10.6 A Cache Hit Was Costing a Commit (the LRU Stamp, and the Stat, on the Read Path)

Found by decomposing the icon, \~95% of Phase 2 and never broken down. Probes inside the icon path (the thumbnail-cache read, the sidecar develop preview, the loader loop, the scale, the rotate and the cache write) answered it on the first run:

```
  [PERF] Phase2 icons  icons=3  cacheHit=1034  cacheMiss=3  cacheGet(ms)=283114.0
                       devThumb(ms)=0.5  load(ms)=0.5  scale(ms)=0.1  orient(ms)=0.0
```

Three icons were DECODED; everything else came out of the thumbnail cache, and reading 1,034 of them cost 283 SECONDS of accumulated thread time across the reader pool (\~274 ms per hit), against 0.5 ms for the three decoded from the file. The load was queueing to read thumbnails.

- One UPDATE on the read path. ThumbCache::get() refreshed the row's LRU `used` stamp on every hit, a WRITE inside the read, under the mutex every reader shares. In WAL every statement outside an explicit transaction is its own commit, exactly the cost writeBatch() was written to avoid ("committing per row is what made the inline version cost 14 ms an icon"); the same mistake made on the other side, where nobody was looking.
- A hit was written straight back. Reader::readIcon called putImage for every icon it produced, including the ones getImage had just handed it. writeBatch skipped them (containsLocked), but getting that far meant taking the mutex the writer holds for a whole batch transaction.

Measured, 1,048 Sony ARW with the cache warm, Phase 2 wall:

```
  before   25,136 ms      cacheGet 283,114 ms   thumbCache(put) 161,144 ms
  after       704 ms      cacheGet   1,063 ms   thumbCache(put)       0 ms
```

36x. The "\~20 ms per thumbnail" was never decode cost; it was lock wait.

The stamp was then moved off the read path entirely (to the writer thread). That was right on its own terms but changed nothing measurable, because the stamps were already fresh (lruStamps = 0 in the run that was supposed to prove it).

What cacheGet actually costs: probing a hit's four parts under a SATURATED pipeline (scrolling during a filter change, \~12 Reader threads on the cores) gave per hit stat 1,870 us, lockWait 10,166 us, sql 210 us, decode 841 us, which reads as a lock disaster. The SAME code on a quiet scroll gave stat 73 us, lockWait 345 us, sql 52 us, decode 263 us, with the mutex HOLD time at every other site measured as 0.0 ms. Nobody was holding the lock in either case. A plain stat() does not vary 25x between two runs over the same files: these are wall-clock measurements on worker threads being descheduled, and under load every figure inflates together.

The lesson is about the instrument. Summed-across-threads wall clock is right for comparing parts of the same run to EACH OTHER (what the Phase2 icons line was built for), and wrong for asking whether a part is expensive in absolute terms, because a busy machine bills scheduling delay to whatever line is timing. What settled it was a QUIET window doing the same work, and hold-time probes that turn "the readers waited" into "and here is who they waited for": an accounting that has to balance.

Kept, behind G::isPerfProbe: the phase timer on MW::filterChange, and the cache hit split on the scroll line (hits, then stat / lockWait / sql / decode / lruStamps per hit), the only view of the thumbnail cache under an idle GUI thread (the Phase2 icons line is emitted once per load from MetaRead::allFinished). Removed once they had answered: the invalidate/compile split and its rowsInserted BLOCK counters, the per-row filterAcceptsRow timer, the mutex hold-time probes, and the wait/scrollToRow/updateIconRange split inside scrollToCurrentRowIfNotVisible; the code to re-derive them is in the history.

At the time, mMutex was recorded as still over-locked (a global serialiser over per-thread handles, which a WAL SELECT does not need) and left alone at \~1 ms an icon. The next section is where that stopped being small.

#### 5.10.7 The Mutex Was the Queue (a WAL Read Needs No Lock, and a Zero-Timer Batches Nothing)

Opening the CATALOG scope with "cache thumbs just in time" OFF reads the whole scope rather than a few screens, and 1 ms an icon over 9,767 hits is not a rounding error:

```
  [PERF] Phase2 icons  icons=0  cacheHit=9767  cacheMiss=22  cacheGet(ms)=304009.2
         cache hit split:  stat(ms)=178.3  lockWait(ms)=299780.9  sql(ms)=347.2  decode(ms)=3608.4
```

Phase 2 took 17.3 s for a scope whose thumbnails were all stored, and 98.6% of the accumulated hit time was the WAIT for mMutex against 0.35 s for the SELECT it protected: 300 s of waiting cannot be explained by 0.35 s of work.

1. The read path stopped locking (see [5.8.3 Locking and the Read Path](#583-locking-and-the-read-path)).
2. The stamp "batch" was one row. The earlier move had batched it with QTimer::singleShot(0), which fires as soon as the writer's loop is idle, so with hits arriving one at a time it fired after every stamp: the per-hit WAL commit was still happening, on another thread, under the same mutex. Stamps now coalesce on a 2 s timer. A batching timer whose delay is zero is a batching timer only when the consumer is behind.
3. The queue moved, which is why the writer side had to be probed. The next run:

```
  [PERF] Phase2 icons  icons=386  cacheHit=18732  cacheMiss=408  cacheGet(ms)=63333.1
         load(ms)=8554.6  thumbCache(ms)=251732.4
         cache hit split:  stat(ms)=523.3  lockWait(ms)=54077.1  sql(ms)=1413.8  decode(ms)=7127.1
         writer:  hold(ms)=36480.5  lruStamps=2355  stampBatches=52
```

```
 thumbCache is the PUT side: 794 puts for 251.7 s, 317 ms each to hand a QImage to another thread. putImage took mMutex to read the mWriter POINTER, so it queued behind the writer's transaction (36.5 s of hold). Waiters need a holder; the "writer: hold / lruStamps / stampBatches" line (G::probeThumbWriterHoldNs, probeThumbStampBatches) is what named it. The handle became an atomic and the encode moved out of the lock.
```

Measured, the same 43,070-row catalog open with JIT thumbnails off (the same 9,767 hits and 22 misses):

```
  before   cacheGet 304,009.2 ms   stat 178.3   lockWait 299,780.9   sql 347.2   decode 3,608.4
  after    cacheGet   4,763.4 ms   stat 243.3   lockWait       0.0   sql 567.7   decode 3,855.0
```

64x, with lockWait gone entirely. (Two runs of the after case, the second on a clean rebuild, gave 5,032 and 4,763 ms: that spread is this measurement's run-to-run noise, worth knowing before reading 5% off a future comparison.) 79% of a hit is now the JPEG decode, the shape a cache read is supposed to have. stat and sql went UP in absolute terms while the total fell by 299 s: threads that no longer wait get scheduled more work per unit of wall clock.

The setting ("Cache thumbs just in time" off) is the honest cause of the load being large, and turning it back on made the symptom go away without touching the defect. The setting decides HOW MANY thumbnails are read; this was about what each one cost.

That made four load-pipeline assumptions overturned by measurement on this work: the centralMsg repaint, "keywords are most of the saving", the \~20 ms metadata read, and this.

#### 5.10.8 Selecting an Image Rebuilt Two Views, per Cached Image (the Click That Stalled)

Open a catalog scope, scroll, click a thumbnail, and the loupe takes seconds to show the image. The GUI stall watchdog reported 2,276 ms and then 1,985 ms across one click, while every probe on the icon path said there was nothing to do (icons set 0.3 ms, the emit flushes 18.8 ms, the reader queue empty). The cost was in what a SELECTION sets off, charged per image entering the image cache rather than per click, which is why it only bit where the cache refills into a large model.

Every image added to or removed from the image cache reaches the GUI as DataModel::setCached, which wrote through sf->setData and then emitted refreshViewsOnCacheChange, which called IconView::refreshIcon on BOTH thumbView and gridView. refreshIcon called forceFullRefresh (rejustify() or setThumbParameters(), which relayouts the view, EMPTIES the delegate's icon cache so every visible thumbnail must be rendered again, and calls MW::updateIconRange, which can move the icon chunk and set MetaRead dispatching) and then QAbstractItemView::dataChanged for the one index (on macOS then, a whole-table accessibility rebuild at \~27 ms). The unblocked sf->setData in setCached was a third notification, and the last un-throttled proxy write left in the model, the one the image cache uses.

Nothing about a badge moves a cell. A cache badge, a rotation and the loupe rectangle are all drawn by the delegate at paint time. refreshIcon now drops THIS row's delegate cache entry, returns without a repaint when the row is not on screen, and otherwise calls update(idx) for that one cell. setCached writes under a QSignalBlocker and schedules the same coalesced, visible-only emit as setValSf.

The shape, for the fourth time: a per-item operation that quietly does whole-model work (the filter tree recompiling per item, MetaRead re-dispatching per redo, the accessibility bridge rebuilding per write, a view relayout per cached image), invisible on a folder and quadratic on a catalog. The probe that survives is a phase timer on MW::fileSelectionChange (menus / scrollSync / loadImage / loupeDisplay / cachePos / infoView / progress), behind G::isPerfProbe and printed only when a selection costs 100 ms or more. The click path had no instrumentation of its own, which is why the answer had to be found by reading the code the icon probes were exonerating.

## 6 Scrolling

### 6.1 View Sync

When the user scrolls a DataModel view (thumbView, gridView or tableView), the scrollbar's valueChanged reaches MW::thumbHasScrolled, gridHasScrolled or tableHasScrolled:

1. MW::updateIconRange measures the first, middle and last visible items (IconView::updateVisible, TableView::updateVisible) and adjusts the icon chunk around the middle visible row (see [5.6 Icon Loading Rules](#56-icon-loading-rules)).
2. The other views are scrolled to sync with the source view's middle visible row, through dm->scrollToIcon. Only a VISIBLE view may write it.
3. MW::updateChange re-dispatches MetaRead for any missing icons in the chunk; orphaned icons outside it are evicted.

Syncing the views would generate more scrollbar signals and loop. G::ScrollSignalGuard (RAII) suppresses the handlers while code scrolls the views itself, in the sync and in fileSelectionChange, where the visible views are scrolled to centre on the current selection. Never set G::ignoreScrollSignal by hand (see [4.7.4 The Visible Range Is Measured After Every Selection](#474-the-visible-range-is-measured-after-every-selection)).

#### 6.1.1 Shift-Extended Selection Looks Ahead

Shift + a navigation key (extending a selection) does not move the current index, so the centre-on-current scroll does not fire. Instead Selection::select (Shift branch) follows the extending selection: it scrolls the visible view(s) just enough to expose the cell one beyond the new selection edge, in the direction of extension (the "look-ahead" cell), so both the last selected item and the next one are visible. It uses EnsureVisible (not centre), so it is a no-op when the look-ahead cell is already on screen, and it is clamped to the start/end of the DataModel. See IconView::ensureRowVisible and TableView::ensureRowVisible.

#### 6.1.2 Painting Delays

When the user changes modes (e.g. Grid to Loupe), an IconView can change from hidden to visible, and a hidden widget cannot be measured, so scrolling to the current index must wait until the view is visible and laid out. A resize (a gridView cell-size change that needs justification, a thumbDock splitter move, a window resize) likewise needs the scrollbar range settled before scrolling.

The view switches do this synchronously: they activate the main window's layout and re-apply the stacked layout's rect so the new page is sized at once, and QListView's posted item layout is forced by scrollTo itself (see [6.4.1.2 The View Switches' Waits (2026-10-01)](#6412-the-view-switches-waits-2026-10-01)). The old IconView::waitUntilScrollReady helper and the G::wait pumps are gone.

### 6.2 Wheel and Trackpad Scrolling

IconView::wheelEvent hijacks trackpad and mouse wheel events and never calls QListView::wheelEvent for them. The two devices take different engines, told apart by the scroll PHASE: phase() == Qt::NoScrollPhase is a wheel; a trackpad gesture always carries a phase (ScrollBegin / Update / End / Momentum).

Two other tests were tried and BOTH failed on a real wheel, each letting every wheel event reach the kinetic engine. Do not reinstate either:

- pixelDelta().isNull(): macOS sets hasPreciseScrollingDeltas for many mice and Qt then fills in BOTH deltas. Measured: pixelDelta (0,-13), angleDelta (0,-26) for one click.
- source() == Qt::MouseEventNotSynthesized: a wheel can arrive as Qt::MouseEventSynthesizedBySystem (the test mouse does), so this excludes the very device it was meant to catch.

G::isWheelProbe logs what the device actually sends (source, phase, both deltas), the distance per click and which engine handled the event. It established the facts in this section and is the first thing to turn on if wheel behaviour is ever wrong again; do not reason about what a device "should" report.

#### 6.2.1 Trackpad: the Kinetic Engine

The delta (pixelDelta) is turned into a per-axis velocity, keeping only the peak speed so the OS momentum tail is absorbed rather than added, and IconView::applyKineticScroll drives both scrollbars from that velocity on a 16 ms timer with friction (kineticFriction 0.99) plus a linear drag, so the glide comes to a clean stop. A zero-delta ScrollBegin (fingers planted on the glass) stops the glide: tap-to-stop. The kinetic engine keeps its own tuned constants and is not affected by the sensitivity preference.

#### 6.2.2 Mouse Wheel: Click Mode

A mouse wheel does NOT feed the kinetic engine. IconView::wheelEvent routes it to IconView::wheelClickScroll, which scrolls a distance per click set by Preferences > "Mouse wheel / trackpad sensitivity" (G::wheelSensitivity). A kinetic flick velocity used to ignore the preference entirely and send a single click gliding for hundreds of thumbnails.

One event is one click: only the sign of the delta is used, never its size. Measured on a real wheel, one slow click is an angleDelta of 24-26 (not the nominal 120 per notch), and macOS scroll acceleration inflates the same click to 444 when spinning fast, a 17x spread for identical physical input. Scaling by it would make the amount depend on spin speed; spinning faster already scrolls faster because it produces more events per second.

The preference drives both halves of the feel, and these two functions are where it is tuned:

- IconView::clickScrollPixels sets the DISTANCE per click, in thumbnail cells (getCellSize), so a click moves a meaningful number of thumbnails whatever the thumb size: 4 cells at 100% sensitivity, 1/4 cell at 1%, a bit over 2 cells at the default 50%.
- IconView::clickScrollRestMs sets the REST TIME, how long one click takes to coast to a stop: 2000 ms at 100%, 500 ms at 1%.

Each click adds to the distance still pending, and IconView::applyClickScroll eases into it on a 16 ms timer, taking a fraction of the remainder per tick. IconView::clickScrollEase derives the per-tick damping from the rest time: the pending distance decays geometrically (after n ticks, distance \* (1 - ease)^n is left, and it stops below the half pixel it cannot render), so solving for ease at n = rest / 16 lands a click on the requested time. The ease depends on the DISTANCE (a 4-cell click must decay more slowly than a quarter-cell one to last as long), so it is computed once per click and held in clickEase. Measured against the real decay loop at a 120 px cell: 1% = 512 ms, 50% = 1248 ms, 100% = 2016 ms, each within a tick of target.

- applyClickScroll puts NO floor on the step size. A sub-pixel step accumulates in clickAccumulator and emerges as a whole pixel a few ticks later; finishing early whenever the step fell below a pixel (the first version) cut the tail off and stopped about a quarter sooner than asked.
- A click in the opposite direction to a scroll already in progress (a click glide or a trackpad glide) stops that scroll and does nothing else; the next click scrolls in the new direction. IconView::scrollInProgress reports the signed motion of whichever engine is running, and IconView::stopScrolling halts both (tap-to-stop calls it too).
- Both mappings share IconView::wheelSensitivityT, which normalises the percent to 0.0 (most sensitive) - 1.0 (least).

G::wheelSensitivity is a PERCENT of maximum sensitivity, 1-100, larger = more sensitive. It used to be 1-210 on the opposite scale, which read backwards in the preferences slider. Loupe and video view, where the preference is the amount of spinning required before the next image and larger must mean LESS sensitive, go through G::wheelSpinThreshold(), which inverts the percent back onto the 1-210 range those views were tuned on (ImageView: ms between advances; VideoView: accumulated angle delta). The QSettings key is wheelSensitivityPct; MW::loadSettings converts a stored wheelSensitivity from the old scale and MW::writeSettings removes it, so an existing user keeps the feel they had.

#### 6.2.3 The Horizontal Thumbnail Row
