WorkingImageCache::render / renderStack do this from the base (scope 0) params; RawFormat::Decode does it from its `edit` argument, falling back to None when there is no recipe.

#### 11.1.3 Wiring

- Non-raw: ImageDecoder::load() decodes to QImage; ImageDecoder::applyDevelop() (after rotate(), before colorManage()) does InputTransform -> Develop -> OutputTransform. It is skipped entirely when EditParams is identity, so the unedited browsing path never round-trips through the float buffer. When it does run it goes through the WorkingImage cache (reuses / populates the pre-develop image).
- Raw: RawFormat::Decode() develops in its native linear float (RawColor::ToCameraNative -> Develop -> OutputTransform), hands its pre-develop WorkingImage back via outWork (cached by ImageDecoder), and ImageDecoder sets developApplied so applyDevelop() does not run a second time.

Abort: RawFormat::Decode() takes the decoder's abort atomic and polls it between stages and once per row inside the demosaic loop, returning false (lastError "Aborted"). ImageCache::stop() (quit) uses a BlockingQueuedConnection to each decoder; without polling, an in-flight 24 MP demosaic would run to completion while the main thread blocks (a beachball). ImageCache::stop() also calls decoders[id]->abortProcessing() (sets the atomic, non-blocking) BEFORE that blocking wait, so the in-flight decode actually sees the flag.

G::useRaw: ImageDecoder::load() attempts the raw path only when G::useRaw is true; when false it skips RawFormat entirely and shows the embedded preview. The operation mode owns it (Develop on, Preview off; see [2.7 Operation Mode (Preview vs Develop)](#27-operation-mode-preview-vs-develop)), and it persists as QSettings "useRaw". The raw decode is also gated by RawFormat::Create() returning a decoder for the extension (arw / dng / cr2 / cr3 / nef / orf / rw2 / raf; others -> embedded JPG). Saved Develop edits are gated on it too: MW::applyDevelopPreviewIfEdited() overlays a non-identity EditStack onto the loupe only when useRaw is on, since the edits are calibrated against the demosaiced raw render; in Preview a developed image is shown from its devPreview instead (see [12.6 Read Paths](#126-read-paths)).

### 11.2 Tone Mapping (the View Transform)

A scene-referred raw render is radiometrically linear and lands dark and flat next to a camera JPEG (measured \~+0.7 EV and much less contrast on the A9 II), so it needs tone mapping. WorkingImage carries a sceneReferred flag: RawColor sets it true (sensor data, with highlight headroom and NO clamp), InputTransform sets it false (a JPEG already has the camera tone curve baked in).

The output stage is THREE composable steps (view transform, then output primaries, then transfer function), of which only the first is a creative decision; the other two are colour management. A view transform TONE-MAPS, so it is forced to None for display-referred input; that rule lives in EffectiveView() and callers never special-case it, which is why the unedited-JPEG round trip stays identity. The view transform used to be a hard-coded constant applied unconditionally to scene-referred data (the app's entire look was one number nobody could choose); making it a value is what let more transforms be added as data.

OutputTransform::ViewTransform, in the "Tone mapping" combo's order:

```
Label (UI)                            Enum (value)        What it is
Standard roll-off                     Filmic (1)          THE DEFAULT. Exposure x kBaselineExposure, then the ACES
                                                          (Narkowicz) shoulder, per channel, in linear before the
                                                          transfer. Lifts midtones, rolls highlights off smoothly.
Standard roll-off (hue-preserving)    FilmicHue (5)       Filmic's curve applied with the DNG SDK's RGBTone (below).
Soft roll-off                         AgX (2)             Wide latitude, for HIGHLIGHT HUE INTEGRITY (below).
Camera contrast                       CameraContrast (3)  The camera MAKER's average curve below a knee, Winnow's
                                                          roll-off above it (below).
Profile curve                         ProfileCurve (4)    The selected profile's own ProfileToneCurve with the same
                                                          roll-off; renders as Standard roll-off when the profile
                                                          carries none (see [[The Look Moved to the Output Stage]]).
---------
None                                  None (0)            THE IDENTITY: scene-linear straight to the transfer function.
```

#### 11.2.1 The Transforms

AgX (Soft roll-off): inset the primaries toward the achromatic axis, run the curve in that compressed space over a 16.5-stop log2 window, outset back. Because the curve runs where the primaries are pulled together, a bright saturated colour desaturates smoothly toward white instead of losing its channels one at a time, which is where per-channel filmic's hue march comes from (saturated red to orange, blue to purple), and why a brightened mask core under Filmic can clip to a flat patch, destroying the falloff calibrated in maskfalloff.h.

- Provenance: the inset matrix and the log2 window are AgX's published constants; THE SIGMOID IS OURS (two power segments meeting at the mid-grey pivot, written rather than ported, so no third-party licence rides along). It is AgX's structure and behaviour, not a bit-exact reproduction of any AgX build.
- With no reference to diff against, tst_outputtransform pins the properties it is CHOSEN for: 18% scene grey renders as 18% display grey (the anchor: if the pivot drifts, every exposure the user has dialled changes meaning), neutrals stay neutral, the curve is monotonic across the whole window, and a saturated colour driven up in exposure desaturates with its off-channels rising TOGETHER (a spread between them is a hue shift).
- The published inset's rows sum to 1 +/- 1.4e-4, so the code normalises them: 0.014% is a tint on every neutral that no white balance can remove.
- Both of those last two are asserted at 16 BITS, deliberately: at 8 bits a mis-derived pivot lands one level away and slips through a within-one tolerance, and the un-normalised rows are 0.04 of a level. Both were measured passing an 8-bit version of the assertion before it was tightened. When an invariant's error is smaller than one part in 255, assert it through ToImage16, which runs the exact maths rather than the 8-bit table.

Camera contrast (added 2026-10-03): Develop/cameracurve.h + Develop/cameracurvedata.h, GENERATED by tools/gen_camera_curves.py from the installed Adobe camera-matching profiles: per maker, every "Camera Standard" ("Camera Natural" for Olympus/OM) composed with its BaselineExposureOffset and averaged; GENERIC = the mean of Canon / Nikon / Sony, used for Fujifilm and any unlisted maker. The maker is the first word of the canonical camera model ("OM" counts as Olympus).

- The shape: y = C(u) below the knee (u = gain\*x; the camera curve exactly as written, so shadows and midtones carry its contrast), and above it y = yk + (1-yk)\*(1 - (1+t)^-p) with t = s\*(u-uk)/(p\*(1-yk)), s = C'(uk): C1 at the knee, monotonic, asymptotic to white.
- kKneeY = 0.60 (output), kTailPower = 0.6, chosen against Standard roll-off by display level (generic / D7200 Camera Neutral / Filmic): sensor white 237/235/236, 2x 244/243/247, 4x 248/247/253, 8x 250/250/255, 64x 254/254/255. Sensor white lands where Standard roll-off puts it, with a GENTLER tail above (Filmic clips by 2.6 stops over). The first attempt (knee 0.80, a 1/t tail) put sensor white at \~250 and squeezed 1.4x..3.8x white into levels 250..254 (the +3 EV face still nearly flat white); tst_inputprofile::profileCurveRollsOffAPushedExposure caught it. Not fitted to a Lightroom render; refit if one says otherwise.
- Why one curve per maker, not per style (measured 2026-10-03 over \~900 installed Camera profiles): within one maker, the Standard / Vivid / Landscape / Portrait curves differ by &lt;= 0.02 above the deep shadows (Canon's three are identical); what makes Camera Vivid vivid is its LookTable, its colour grade. Across makers they differ more (Canon flatter: 0.405 at x=0.18 vs Nikon 0.448), and across bodies of one maker by up to 0.07-0.12. So: ONE camera-contrast curve per maker, and the styles' colour from Profile.

The camera curves, FilmicHue and Profile curve are applied HUE-PRESERVINGLY (CameraCurve::ApplyRGBTone, the SDK's RGBTone: the brightest and darkest channel take the curve, the middle one is interpolated), not per channel, so they take OutputTransform's per-pixel CAMERA PATH rather than the 1-D tables. That path is also what a profile LookTable needs; everything without either keeps the table paths, so Standard roll-off on an image with no look renders bit-for-bit as before. DisplayPosition (tone-region handle placement) has no image, so for both camera curves it uses the GENERIC curve per channel (the maker curves sit within a few levels of it).

Standard roll-off (hue-preserving), added 2026-10-10: Filmic's curve (FilmicTone) tabulated as a CameraCurve::Curve (FilmicCurve() in outputtransform.cpp, on the camera curves' log2 window) and applied with ApplyRGBTone in the working space (Rec.2020). Neutrals render exactly as Standard roll-off (equal channels make RGBTone the per-channel curve).

- Why: measured pixel-aligned against Lightroom Classic on an E-M1 snow raw (Adobe Standard, As Shot, Exposure 0; the Winnow export warped onto Lightroom's lens-corrected geometry, 0.41 px RMS over 5,070 SIFT matches), per-channel Standard roll-off turned bright blues toward cyan (hue error -11 deg at L\* 60-70, -19 deg at 70-90, a\* -4.7), because the shoulder compresses the high blue channel more than green. A model of exactly that (undo Lightroom's hue-preserving curve, re-apply per channel) predicted the error. Hue-preserving cut it to -1.6 / -1.9 / -4.5 deg (a\* -0.7), saturated colours (C\* 30-80) from -16 / -7 deg to -2 / -2, and the frame's mean dE76 from 4.84 to 4.37 (p90 10.3 -> 8.2). The FilmicHue render was DERIVED from the Standard roll-off export (invert the per-channel curve in Rec.2020, re-apply with RGBTone), a route validated against Winnow's own OutputTransform on 1,974 random colours (p99 0.055 levels of 255).
- Cost: bright saturated colours keep \~5-10% more chroma than Lightroom (they no longer fade toward white the per-channel way).
- Still open, not fixed by it: shadows (L\* &lt; 30) 1.2-2.4 L\* lighter and redder than Lightroom (hue +6..+9 deg, a\* +0.7..+1.2); near-neutral tint (chroma &lt; 5: 2.6 in Lightroom, 5.7 in Winnow); whites (L\* > 80) 1.7-2.7 L\* darker. (Lens distortion correction has since been added; see [11.24 Lens Profile (lensfun)](#1124-lens-profile-lensfun).)
- An option, NOT the default. EditStack::sanitizeParams' range check covers it (up to 5). Tested by tst_outputtransform::filmicHueKeepsNeutralsAndHue (greys equal to Filmic; a sky blue pushed 3 stops drifts 5.2 deg against Filmic's 19.1) and tst_inputprofile (enum value pinned).

#### 11.2.2 The Filmic Fit (kBaselineExposure and the Toe)

Develop/outputtransform.cpp, FilmicTone, as refitted 2026-10-04: kBaselineExposure 2.869, toe b 0.2166 and e 1.0550; the shoulder a, c, d unchanged, so the shape and the roll-off stay. The curve reaches white at v = 2.318, so kToneDomainMax = 2.35.

Per-camera baseline exposure is applied at STAGE 0. Camera Raw's exposure ramp is Exposure + TotalBaselineExposure (dng_render.cpp), a per-body value from Adobe's camera database: +0.15 EV on an ILCE-1/ILCE-1M2, +0.35 on an A9 II, D7200 or most full-frame bodies, from -0.78 (Leica M10, early Nikons) to +1.15 (Fujifilm X-T2) across 25 sampled bodies. Winnow folds it into Develop::InputMatrix (applied exactly once per image, so a mask layer cannot add it twice, and before the LookTable, as in the SDK).

- Values: Develop/baselineexposuredata.h, GENERATED by tools/gen_baseline_exposure.py (one sample raw per body through a CURRENT Adobe DNG Converter, reading the DNG's UniqueCameraModel + BaselineExposure; an old 2017 converter refused the ILCE-1).
- Lookup (Develop/baselineexposure.h): case-insensitive on the canonical model, Olympus &lt;-> "OM Digital Solutions" both ways; an UNLISTED body gets +0.35 (the commonest value); an EMPTY model (non-raw, synthetic test images) gets 0.
- The Apple Core Image engine does not pass through stage 0 and is not affected.

kToneDomainMax is derived from the curve's constants and moves with them. The transfer LUT spans 0..kToneDomainMax and clamps to its last entry above that, which is only correct where the curve has already reached white. Lowering the lift without raising the domain is the trap: the table would end where the curve is still short of white, so every value above it renders as the same almost-white byte and the image never reaches 255 (specular highlights lose a stop and a half of separation, with every headroom test still passing because they all sample below the old end). tst_outputtransform::filmicDomainCoversSaturation is the guard: a value just under the domain must still render below 255 and a value past saturation must render exactly 255. It deliberately does not assert a strict rise throughout: 8-bit quantisation legitimately flattens the top.

The golden hashes are the check. tst_outputtransform::outputBytesAreUnchanged pins six renders. When the curve is refitted, the four Filmic ones are regenerated and the other two (sRGB/None/display and sRGB/AgX/scene) must come back BYTE-IDENTICAL, which proves the change reached Filmic and nothing else; a regeneration that moved all six would mean something broader had changed unnoticed.

Existing sidecars DO move when the fit changes, because it changes the RENDERING of the transform itself (every image saved with viewTransform 1 re-renders). Accepted deliberately each time: the alternative is leaving a constant that is measurably wrong. The tone sliders' Lightroom fit is unaffected by a refit (it was measured relative to the zero render).

##### 11.2.2.1 The Calibration Record

How the fit was reached, kept so the next refit does not repeat the mistakes:

- The 2026-10-04 symptom: with Adobe Standard in both apps, a D7200 frame needed about +0.5 EV in Winnow to match Lightroom, faces read "redder", and a low-key ILCE-1 portrait (the camera the 09-17 lift was fitted on) rendered 0.5-0.9 EV darker through the shadows. Two causes, both measured: Adobe's per-camera BaselineExposure (above), which every earlier lift fit had absorbed for ONE camera (most of the "unexplained" 0.43 EV between the 1.6 and 1.191 fits below); and the Narkowicz toe (slope b/e = 0.21 at black) crushing low-key frames, where per-channel curves in that steep region oversaturated skin. After the refit, warm-pixel saturation matches Lightroom within \~0.015 on all frames and hue differences are small and of both signs (D7200 aside, \~4 deg redder; a camera-specific residual).
- Method: Lightroom Classic 15.5 exports in \~/Pictures/\_LRref (Adobe Standard, defaults, LENS CORRECTIONS OFF, because vignetting correction skews whole-frame comparisons badly; 16-bit sRGB): three ILCE-1 frames (low-key portrait, indoor, bright outdoor), an ILCE-1M2 frame with a near-clipped highlight, and a D7200 frame held out. Winnow's scene-linear luminance (after stage 0) quantile-matched against Lightroom's recovers Lightroom's tone curve per image independent of framing; the four Sony frames collapse onto ONE curve within \~1 level once BaselineExposure is applied. A six-free-constant fit was better on paper but reached white AT sensor white (no roll-off) and was rejected.
- Verified end to end through the real pipeline (Adobe Standard including its LookTable), RMS levels of 255 against the Lightroom export, before -> after: ILCE-1 low-key 6.6 -> 1.3, indoor 11.8 -> 1.3, outdoor 12.4 -> 1.4, ILCE-1M2 highlight 12.4 -> 2.2, D7200 (held out) 18.9 -> 2.0.
- The harness (scratch, not in the repo): rawpy/libraw camera-native pixels (half size, no WB, NOT rescaled) fed through RawColor::Characterise + Develop::Apply + OutputTransform::ToImage, linked against the tonecurvedump target's object files; it reproduces an in-app Winnow screenshot to \~0.15 EV. Rebuild it the same way for the next refit.
- The scale trap (cost a refit): an ARW carries TWO white levels, 16383 in the raw IFD (tag 50717) and 15360 in the encrypted SR2 block. Winnow normalises by 16383 deliberately (libraw agrees byte for byte, and Adobe's own DNG of the file says WhiteLevel 16383). The first refit that morning scaled the harness's Sony pixels by 16383/15360, so it fitted pixels 7% brighter than the app's (giving 2.685) and every Sony render came out 0.1 EV dark. Caught by comparing the harness against the APP'S OWN full-size devPreview of the same file (PreviewCache/&lt;hex id>.jpg, id from index.db devpreview by path). Check the harness against an app render FIRST next time.
- Hue after the refit (pixel-ALIGNED against the exports; per-image "warm pixel" masks are biased and must not be used): skin-like pixels, median hue error per-channel / RGBTone: ILCE-1 portrait -1.8 / +0.3 deg, indoor 0.0 / +0.1, outdoor -0.6 / +0.2, ILCE-1M2 +1.4 / +0.5, D7200 +0.5 / +1.9. Saturation identical between the two (within 0.02 of Lightroom); neutrals within +-2.4 deg on every frame, so white balance is right. Adobe Standard's LookTable rotates skin about -8 deg; without it skin would be 6-8 deg too yellow. RGBTone was not made the DEFAULT on this evidence (better on the Sony frames, worse on the D7200, and it costs Standard roll-off its 1-D table fast path); it later shipped as the hue-preserving option on the E-M1 evidence above.
- The older lift: 1.6 (+0.68 EV), validated against an A9 II embedded preview at mean luma 0.434 vs 0.445, was re-measured on 2026-09-17 on a different raw against TWO independent references (that file's embedded preview, and Lightroom's Adobe Standard rendering) and came out \~0.43 EV too bright against BOTH (implied lifts 1.196 and 1.188; joint fit 1.191). Where 1.6 came from is NOT KNOWN, and is recorded as unknown rather than given a plausible story: neither recorded luma is near the test file's preview (100.9) or its 1.6 render (118.8). A first explanation (the embedded preview is a brighter target than Lightroom, so the two calibrations aimed at different references) was WRONG: on that file preview and Lightroom agree to 2.1/255. It is written down because it was confidently stated and it changed the recommendation. The method then, and now: a histogram fit over 99 luminance percentiles, NOT a pixel diff (the exports were framed slightly differently).
- The 2026-09-17 shoulder measurement (ILCE-1, during the tone-region fit) found Winnow's zero render needing gamma 1.42 to agree with Lightroom's Adobe Color and 1.32 with Adobe Standard; the two Lightroom profiles were only 3.24 levels apart, so almost none of the gap was the profile; residual 11.1 levels, best exposure correction -0.06 EV, peaking at +32 levels around p60. That contradicted a 1.2-level figure recorded for Filmic earlier on an unrecoverable frame, and it was recorded unreconciled. The 10-04 refit of the toe and lift is what addressed it.

Known readout inconsistency (not a render bug): with a camera profile selected, the Temp/Tint row shows the as-shot solve from the BUILT-IN matrix (an ILCE-1 frame: 4250 K / +10) while the render uses the profile's (4156 K / +12.9, CameraProfile::resolveAsShot). Lightroom shows its own number again (4450 K). The pixels are unaffected: "as shot" is the camera's neutral either way.

#### 11.2.3 Selecting It

EditParams::viewTransform is an INT (an OutputTransform::ViewTransform cast), like wbPreset, so it rides the existing int machinery (sanitizeParams clamp, kIntFields for multi-image, the preset round trip). THE NUMBERING IS A PUBLISHED FORMAT (0 None, 1 Filmic, 2 AgX, 3 CameraContrast, 4 ProfileCurve, 5 FilmicHue): add freely, never renumber. None is 0 because zero is what an absent or unreadable sidecar field means.

The identity is NOT the default, and this is the only field where they differ. EditParams::kDefaultViewTransform is Filmic (1), the SINGLE place the default is stated: isIdentity() compares against it (never a literal 0), resetGroup(Basic) restores it via def.viewTransform, and sanitizeParams repairs an out-of-range value to it. tst_inputprofile::defaultViewTransformIsFilmic pins the numbering, the default, the reset and both directions of the isIdentity test; viewTransformSanitisesToTheDefault pins the load path.

- History, because the losing argument is the seductive one: Filmic was 0 originally; on 2026-09-13 None was renumbered to 0 and made the default, on the reasoning that the identity must be the default or resets and isIdentity() carry a special case. The reasoning is correct and the conclusion was wrong: with no view transform a scene-referred raw renders dark and flat, so "no edits" was a look nobody would choose. Measured 2026-09-16 against Lightroom's Adobe Standard rendering of the same raw: the untransformed render's luminance spread is two thirds as wide (std 24 vs 36 of 255), its midtone \~0.7 EV low, and fitting each transform to Lightroom's percentiles landed Filmic within 1.2 levels, AgX within 5.3 and None within 6.2. So the default is Filmic and the special case is real, held in one named constant.
- A camera profile does not make it redundant. Adobe Standard carries no curve: every Adobe Standard .dcp sampled has a HueSatMap and a LookTable and NO tone curve, and neither does Winnow Standard. Lightroom supplies its own baseline curve in that case; this is Winnow's.
- Existing sidecars do not move on a default change: paramsToJson writes viewTransform unconditionally, so every sidecar carries an explicit value, None included. Only an image with no sidecar (an untouched raw) picks up the default. A sidecar that OMITS the key falls back to whatever is already in the struct, which is why paramsFromJson must read into a default-constructed EditParams.
- An unknown value resolves to the IDENTITY at render time (OutputTransform::ViewFromInt) rather than failing, so a sidecar from a later build still opens: colour management does not invent a look when it cannot tell what was asked for, and reaching for kDefaultViewTransform there would make the output stage depend on EditParams. Restoring the DEFAULT is the sanitiser's job, one layer up at load.

It is the one EditParams field NOT consumed by Develop::Apply (OutputTransform reads it, three stages later), and it is a WHOLE-IMAGE property: DevelopProperties::setViewTransform always writes SCOPE 0 whatever scope is active (a per-scope value would mean different looks in different parts of one picture). The render sites read it from the params they already receive.

The control is a QComboBox (DevelopProperties::addViewTransformRow) in the value cell of the SECOND ROW OF BASIC, directly under the camera profile, above the divider and white balance, labelled "Tone mapping", modelled on the WB preset row (addItem(name, enum) + activated + findData under a QSignalBlocker). A combo gets no history for free, so setViewTransform calls noteScopeEdit itself. Hovering an entry previews it (see [11.3.1 Hovering the Dropdown Previews](#1131-hovering-the-dropdown-previews)); Profile curve's text and enabled state follow the profile (refreshViewTransformRow).

#### 11.2.4 Naming and Placement

The labels are not the identifiers. The enum values, the sidecar key and every constant keep the names Filmic and AgX (the published names of the transforms, and what the maths implements); the labels say what the options DO, in DevelopProperties::viewTransformName, one function shared by the combo and the History entry so the two can never disagree. Docs/developbasichelp.html names Filmic and AgX explicitly so both terms stay searchable.

- "AgX" (short for silver halide) is guessable by nobody. The rejected candidate "Flat highlight protection" advertised AgX's best-known criticism (it looks flat next to a camera rendering), and "highlight protection" collides with highlight RECOVERY (reconstructing blown detail from sensor headroom, the Highlights slider a few rows below, which this is NOT).
- "Filmic" went in 2026-09-17: the word reads as a CREATIVE choice, a film emulation to opt into, when it is the plain rendering that lands where every other raw developer lands. "Standard roll-off" says "this is the ordinary one" without claiming a match to any camera ("Camera match" would overclaim), and keeps PARALLEL FORM with "Soft roll-off": the two differ by one word, which is their real relationship. The known cost, accepted: the Profile row above reads "Adobe Standard" / "Camera Standard", so "Standard" appears in two adjacent rows meaning different things; the two-word phrase carries it. "Natural roll-off" dodged the collision only by saying nothing; "Photographic" broke the parallel form.
- "Tone mapping", not "View": the identifiers and the sidecar key stay `viewTransform`. "View" is technically correct but Winnow already spends the word on the central widget modes (loupe / grid / table / compare, MW::viewMenu). "Tone mapping" slightly undersells AgX (whose real point is the inset/outset gamut compression), which the tooltip and the help page carry.
- None is LAST, below a separator, a deliberate exception to the rule that an adjustment's identity heads its range. That rule assumes the identity is a neutral starting position; here it is unrendered scene-linear data, dark and flat. The list is ordered by what the user is choosing between (ways of rolling highlights off, then the camera-style pair), with the separator setting None apart as the absence of a rendering, for building a look from scratch (changed 2026-09-17).
- At the head of the tone group: this control sets the overall mapping and the sliders beneath it adjust WITHIN it. A real dependency: the same Exposure value does not mean the same thing under Filmic and AgX, because AgX leaves far more highlight room before anything clips.
- In Basic, not Calibrate (it was briefly in Calibrate). Lightroom's Adobe Color / Camera Standard live in the PROFILE control at the top of BASIC, while Lightroom's CALIBRATION panel is the R/G/B primary rotation, which is what Winnow's Calibrate is. Calibrate runs mid-Develop in linear, the view transform runs last in OutputTransform, so grouping them implies an adjacency that does not exist. And it re-scopes every slider beneath it and is decided early, whereas Calibrate is a rarely opened fine-tuning section. Moving it cost the group bookkeeping the checklist warns about: EditParams::resetGroup's case (Calibrate -> Basic, so Reset Basic and the Basic preview eye cover it) and the preset leaf table (kCalibrateLeaves -> kBasicLeaves). Neither fails to compile if missed.

### 11.3 The Profile and Tone Mapping Rows

Profile is at the TOP of Basic, Lightroom's slot, and Tone mapping sits directly under it, in the same top group (moved there 2026-09-14). The two answer the same question: what rendering is everything below made on top of. Profile characterises the camera and feeds white balance; Tone mapping decides the scene-to-display mapping the tone sliders work within.

```
Profile        [ Camera NT v2    v ]   stage 0: camera characterisation + its look
Tone mapping   [ Standard roll-off v ] output: the mapping the sliders work within
------------------------------------
WB             [dropper] [ As Shot v ]
Temp / Tint
------------------------------------
Exposure / Contrast / Highlights / ...
```

- This one genuinely IS Lightroom's Profile (Adobe Standard / Camera Neutral / Camera Vivid), so a user finds it where they expect. Profile-first is also real DEPENDENCY order: the camera profile feeds the white balance (WhiteBalance::solve walks cam.xyzToCam), so a profile change moves what a given Kelvin means. And it leaves Calibrate as what it is: the manual primary tweak ON TOP of whatever the profile produced, Lightroom's relationship between Calibration and Profile.
- A profile is applied WHOLE; there is no switch for its look. Its bare characterisation is a separate entry, "Camera Base" (see [11.6.8 Camera Bases](#1168-camera-bases)). A profile's own tone curve is offered as a tone mapping choice ("Profile curve"), never forced.
- One row of camera profiles. A separator sits under "Winnow Standard": the built-in is the identity, a different kind of thing from an installed profile. (A second kind of entry, film-look LUTs, briefly shared this row and was removed; the argument for one row, should anything else want a place in it, is in [11.7 Film-Look LUTs (.cube / HaldCLUT): Declined](#117-film-look-luts-cube--haldclut-declined).)
- Gated, with two distinct reasons that are not interchangeable, shown inline in the value cell where the control would be:
  - non-raw: no camera characterisation at all (cam.valid is false) -> "raw only". OutputTransform forces the view transform to None for display-referred input, so Tone mapping on a JPEG would be live and silently do nothing; it reads "raw only" too. currentIsRaw() gates both at build time, as the WB row gates its named illuminants.
  - the Apple Core Image engine: applerawdecode.mm bypasses RawColor and returns pixels with Core Image's own profile applied, so a camera profile is meaningless and must not silently do nothing -> "Apple decoder" (unlike "raw only", it names something the user can change).
- Decided before building: changing the profile changes the camera matrix, so resolveAsShot lands somewhere different. THE STORED NUMBERS ARE HELD and the rendering moves, as Lightroom does. Holding the appearance instead would mean re-solving and silently rewriting numbers the user chose.

#### 11.3.1 Hovering the Dropdown Previews

With the Profile or Tone mapping list open, the item under the cursor (or under the keyboard highlight; `highlighted` is the signal, so arrowing behaves identically) is shown on the loupe. A profile is the one Basic control whose effect cannot be guessed from its name ("Camera VV2 v2" means nothing until you see it), and the list runs to twenty-odd entries.

It reuses the EXISTING preview override the Presets list and History put up (previewStack / previewActive / historyPreviewChanged): the stored stack, the sliders and the history are never touched, and the render is proxy-only with no full-res settle. The machinery is shared, not copied:

- DevelopProperties::armComboHover wires a combo's `highlighted` to ONE debounce timer (comboHoverTimer) that runs whatever action the last highlight left in comboHoverPending, and installs the popup-Hide filter. previewCameraProfile / previewViewTransform each build the preview stack (scope 0) and hand it to showComboHoverPreview. endComboHoverPreview is the single end path, called from each row's activated() and from the queued Hide handler. One flag (comboHoverActive) covers both rows, since only one popup can be open at a time.
- Debounced at 120 ms, the same constant the Presets list uses. A look profile costs \~13 ms of pixel work per tick on top of the rest of the pipeline, so an undebounced sweep queues a render per row.
- The popup's hide is watched, because QComboBox reports a SELECTION and never a dismissal; without it, Esc or a click away leaves the loupe showing a profile the image does not have. The restore is QUEUED: on a click the view hides before activated() is delivered, so ending inline would restore the old profile and have it immediately overwritten (a wasted full render and a visible flash).
- One timer for the life of the panel. These rows are rebuilt with the tree, and a timer created per rebuild would accumulate as a child of the panel, each able to fire a preview for a combo that no longer exists. The pending action holds a QPointer to its combo, since a rebuild can delete it while the debounce is running.
- A greyed "Profile curve (none in this profile)" is not highlightable, so it never previews its fallback.

### 11.4 Output Colour

#### 11.4.1 Widening the Working Space (Rec.709 to Rec.2020)

Rec.709 is narrower than every camera's own gamut, so a saturated sensor colour used to be clipped at DECODE, before the user had touched the image, irrecoverably. It is now carried through to the output stage, the only stage that knows what gamut it renders into. The flip is one line (kWorking), because everything derives from it: the decoder's camera -> working conversion (now stage 0), InputTransform converting on the way in, OutputTransform deriving its primaries matrix from the source tag, and every op reading lumaWeights().

- It was deliberately held at LinearSRGB while the camera -> working conversion moved out of the decoder, so the PLUMBING change and the PIXEL change could be attributed separately; both regressions found during that move were provably not the space.
- It was held further until AgX landed, because preserving wide-gamut data only helps if something compresses it gracefully on the way out; otherwise it just clips per channel at the output matrix instead of at the decode. Under Filmic an out-of-gamut colour is no worse than before, just no better; AgX (and the hue-preserving roll-off) is what makes the wider space pay.
- Tests of a property defined BY a colour space must take the definition from ColorSpaceMath, not restate it. tst_calibrate and tst_colorgrade each carried their own hard-coded Rec.709 luma triple to assert "this op preserves luma" / "this tint has zero luma"; both failed the moment the working space widened, while the ops were still correct.

#### 11.4.2 Output Spaces

OutputTransform::ToImage / ToImage16 take an OutputTransform::Space: sRGB (default), DisplayP3 or AdobeRGB. The conversion is a 3x3 from the working primaries (Rec.2020) to the target primaries, applied in LINEAR after the view transform, then the target's transfer curve: the sRGB piecewise curve for sRGB AND P3 (what the P3 display spec uses), gamma 563/256 = 2.19921875 for Adobe RGB.

- Whoever writes the QImage must TAG it to match, via OutputTransform::ColorSpaceOf(space); a mismatch is worse than no tag at all.
- Validated against Qt's own colour engine as an oracle (QImage::convertedToColorSpace over 11 patches including primaries, greys and near-black): max channel error 0/255 for sRGB and Display P3, 1/255 for Adobe RGB (Qt's fixed-point rounding).
- The space is threaded through WorkingImageCache::render / renderStack (Space, default sRGB) and MW::developComposite / developCompositeStack exactly as OutDepth is, and is chosen per export (see [14 Export](#14-export)).
- Arbitrary destination ICC profiles via Lcms2 remain a later phase.

#### 11.4.3 Two Paths, Neither With a Transcendental

When the primaries matrix is the identity, the whole per-channel chain is 1-D and ONE table replaces it (the fused path, \~4.8x the pow it replaced; see the TRANSFER LUT note in outputtransform.cpp). When it is not, the matrix sits between the view curve and the transfer so the two cannot fuse, and the chain becomes table -> matrix -> rolloff -> table (the split path). With a Rec.2020 working space, sRGB output is no longer an identity matrix, so EVERY render takes the split path; that is why the split path, once export-only and running exact pow maths, had to become table-driven first.

- ViewTransform::None is deliberately NOT tabulated on the split path: its table would stop at 1.0 and clamp away exactly the over-range values HighlightRolloff exists to redistribute (pinned by tst_outputtransform::viewTransformNoneIsPassThrough).
- Hue-preserving curves and profile LookTables take a third, per-pixel CAMERA PATH (see [11.2.1 The Transforms](#1121-the-transforms)).

#### 11.4.4 Highlight Roll-off

OutputTransform::HighlightRolloff is the last step before the transfer curve, in linear and in the OUTPUT primaries, the space the clip happens in. Any channel over 1.0 would otherwise be hard-clipped by Transfer's Clamp01, which made a brightened radial mask look banded: the mask core clipped flat, hiding the smootherstep falloff, which then re-appeared with a derivative kink (a Mach-band ring) where the channel dropped back under 1.0, with a hue swing as the channels clipped one at a time. Instead, the energy the peak channel loses to the clip is BLED into the other two, so an over-range colour desaturates smoothly toward white, the Lightroom behaviour (a green frame pushed past white gives \~(154,255,151) here vs Lightroom's \~(172,255,164), measured).

Pixels at or below white are bit-exact, so unedited images and their exports are untouched; that is why this is a bleed and not a compressive shoulder (any soft knee below 1.0 would darken existing whites). It applies to raw and non-raw alike, in both ToImage and ToImage16.

### 11.5 The WorkingImage Cache

Develop/workingimagecache.h. The expensive part of a raw is UnpackCfa -> Demosaic -> RawColor, which produces the pre-develop WorkingImage; Develop + OutputTransform after it are cheap. So that WorkingImage is cached, and an interactive slider change re-renders through Develop + OutputTransform only, never decoding or demosaicing again.

- Storage: WorkingImageCache::instance().put(fPath, work). A raw caches the pre-develop WorkingImage that RawFormat::Decode() hands back through its outWork out-param (a shared_ptr, no pixel copy; the snapshot is always pre-develop, so a non-identity edit develops on a private copy and leaves the cached image pristine). A non-raw caches the post-InputTransform WorkingImage the first time applyDevelop() builds one.
- Keyed by SOURCE path + raw renderer TAG (see [10.9 Raw Renderers (Winnow and Apple)](#109-raw-renderers-winnow-and-apple)): a master on Winnow and its version on Apple Raw 9 hold separate bases.
- Re-render: WorkingImageCache::get(fPath, tag) + WorkingImageCache::render(work, edit, out). render() is static and stateless: an identity edit converts and outputs (stage 0 still runs on a copy); a non-identity edit copies + Develop + OutputTransform. ImageDecoder::applyDevelop() uses this fast path (a hit skips InputTransform; a miss builds and caches once). The editor calls get() + render() directly; a miss falls back to a full decode, which re-populates the entry.
- Memory: entries are shared_ptr&lt;const WorkingImage> (\~3-4x the 8-bit QImage), so the cache is byte-budgeted (kDefaultMaxBytes 768 MB) with LRU eviction; the most recently used entry is never evicted, and the Develop pin keeps the image being edited (every renderer's entry for it). It is a small edit accelerator for recently viewed images, NOT a second image cache, and is not counted by the image cache's sizeMB (see [5.7 Memory Governor (Process Footprint, Decode Concurrency)](#57-memory-governor-process-footprint-decode-concurrency)). ImageCache::initialize() clear()s it on every folder change.
- The live drag renders a downscaled proxy and the full-resolution settle render runs async off the GUI thread (renderDevelopFullResAsync); see [11.12 Develop Performance](#1112-develop-performance).

EditParams is the per-scope unit; the editor renders an EditStack of a Global scope plus mask scopes (see [11.15 Scope and Mask Model](#1115-scope-and-mask-model)), and the op maths is the same for each.

### 11.6 Camera Profiles (DCP)

All four slices are built (2026-09-13; the look reworked 2026-09-14 and re-ordered 2026-10-03). This section records what a Lightroom camera profile IS, so the implementation is read off the DNG spec rather than guessed. The UI is in [11.3 The Profile and Tone Mapping Rows](#113-the-profile-and-tone-mapping-rows).

#### 11.6.1 What a Profile Is

A DCP (DNG Camera Profile) is a small TIFF-structured file built out of DNG tag numbers, or the same tags embedded directly in a DNG. It is NOT an ICC profile: an ICC input profile characterises a camera under ONE illuminant, whereas a DCP carries TWO calibrations and interpolates between them at render time using the shot's own white balance. That is why a DCP tracks mixed and unusual lighting better, and why Lightroom's Profile control and its Temp slider are coupled.

How Adobe makes one: a colour target (ColorChecker 24 / SG, sometimes a much larger chart) is shot with the specific camera MODEL under two illuminants, normally Standard Illuminant A (\~2856 K tungsten) and D65, or the equivalent is derived from measured spectral sensitivities. For each illuminant a 3x3 XYZ -> camera raw RGB mapping is least-squares fitted over the patches. A 3x3 cannot fit a real sensor (metameric error is nonlinear), so the residual per-patch error is baked into a 3-D HSV lookup table: for a grid of hue x saturation x value, a (hue shift in degrees, saturation scale, value scale) triple. THAT TABLE is what makes "Adobe Standard" look like Adobe Standard rather than a bare matrix, and it is the part most third-party raw developers omit. The camera-matching looks (Camera Vivid, Camera Portrait, Camera Neutral) are the same colorimetric base plus a SECOND table of the same form and a tone curve, hand-tuned to imitate the manufacturer's JPEG.

What is in the file:

- Identity and licence: UniqueCameraModel, ProfileName, ProfileCopyright, ProfileEmbedPolicy.
- Calibration: CalibrationIlluminant1/2 (EXIF light-source codes, e.g. 17 = Standard A, 21 = D65); ColorMatrix1/2 (XYZ -> camera, per illuminant, used to ESTIMATE the illuminant from the as-shot neutral); ForwardMatrix1/2 (camera -> XYZ at D50, constructed so a white-balanced camera neutral maps EXACTLY to D50, used for RENDERING); CameraCalibration1/2 and AnalogBalance (per-individual-unit correction, almost always identity).
- Tables: ProfileHueSatMapData1/2 with Dims and Encoding (the baseline correction), ProfileLookTableData with Dims and Encoding (the creative look, same form), ProfileToneCurve (the look's tone curve).
- Offsets the look assumes: BaselineExposureOffset, DefaultBlackRender.

The two matrix families are not interchangeable, and confusing them is the classic DCP bug: ColorMatrix runs XYZ -> camera and exists to SOLVE for the illuminant; ForwardMatrix runs camera -> XYZ and exists to RENDER. A profile may ship without ForwardMatrix, in which case it is derived from the inverse of ColorMatrix with a Bradford adaptation to D50, so the renderer needs both paths.

The DNG render order (spec 1.4+): linearise -> demosaic -> white balance by the camera neutral (times CameraCalibration and AnalogBalance) -> interpolate the two illuminants and apply ForwardMatrix -> XYZ D50 -> ProPhoto linear -> HueSatMap applied in HSV -> exposure and tone -> LookTable -> ProfileToneCurve (dng_render.cpp ProcessArea: HueSatMap -> exposure ramp (user exposure + BaselineExposureOffset) -> LookTable -> RefBaselineRGBTone). The first two steps are RawFormat::Decode; the white balance and matrix are stage 0; the HueSatMap is stage 0.5; the look is in OutputTransform.

Why this is cheap here: WorkingImageCache holds CAMERA-NATIVE pixels, so a profile change is a RE-RENDER, never a re-decode, and the whole matrix half of a profile folds into the single 3x3 buildPointCoeffs already computes. Only the tables add work.

#### 11.6.2 The Parser (ImageFormats/Dcp)

A DCP is a TIFF whose magic word is 0x4352 instead of 42, with one IFD and no image data, so it reuses TiffWalk::Reader (the raw decoders' walk) and adds only tag interpretation. Direct C++, no exiftool. Dcp::Profile is a plain struct: QString for the four text tags, Matrix3 (float[3][3], the convention of CameraColor::xyzToCam), Table3D for the tables. parseFile() reads a standalone .dcp; parseIfd() reads the identical tags in IFD0 of a DNG. Dcp::peek() reads ONLY the two identifying strings. Unit test tests/unit/tst_dcp.cpp.

- Absence is a fact. Every optional tag has a have\* flag beside it rather than a default value, because "missing" and "identity" render identically wrong: a profile with no ForwardMatrix is legal (1 of 313 real profiles swept), and the renderer must derive one rather than multiply by an identity. A malformed tag is an ERROR, not an absence (a ColorMatrix with 8 values is a corrupt file).
- Tag numbers were verified, not recalled: ProfileHueSatMapEncoding = 51107, ProfileLookTableEncoding = 51108, BaselineExposureOffset = 51109, DefaultBlackRender = 51110 (widely misremembered as 51089/51090, which the first draft of the plan carried).
- One dims tag, two tables: ProfileHueSatMapDims (50937) is SHARED by Data1 and Data2, which is what makes interpolating the two entry by entry legal. Presence is keyed on the DATA tag: a single-illuminant profile carries the dims and Data1 with no Data2. Pinned by tst_dcp::singleIlluminantProfileParses.
- The two families carry different tables (measured over the 4,373 installed profiles): "Adobe Standard" carries a HueSatMap and NO LookTable; "Camera \*" profiles carry a LookTable and NO HueSatMap. The test sweeps real profiles STRIDE-SAMPLED across the sorted tree; the first version took the first 400, all from one folder, and reported the other family's table as universally absent while the parser was reading it correctly.
- Not read, deliberately: the DNG 1.6 third illuminant (52529 / 52531 / 52532 / 52537) and its spectral IlluminantData; its presence is REPORTED (Profile::hasThirdIlluminant) so the renderer can say a profile exceeds what is supported. Nor ExtraCameraProfiles (50933), the pointer array to further profile IFDs inside a DNG.

#### 11.6.3 The Matrix Path

Develop/cameraprofile.h/.cpp (tests/unit/tst_cameraprofile.cpp). CameraProfile::camToWorking(profile, kelvin, tint) returns the one 3x3 that fills CameraColor::camToWorking, so it folds into PointCoeffs::preMat and costs NO extra per-pixel work.

```
camera RGB
  -> inv(AnalogBalance . CameraCalibration)      undo the per-INDIVIDUAL-camera correction (usually identity)
  -> diag(1 / referenceNeutral)                   the WHITE BALANCE
  -> ForwardMatrix                                camera -> XYZ, landing on D50
  -> Bradford D50 -> the working space's white    the one adaptation in the pipeline
  -> XYZ -> working primaries
= working RGB
```

- The white balance is INSIDE the matrix. The built-in (dcraw-style) path is a FIXED matrix with per-channel gains in front; under DNG the chosen white picks the interpolation weight AND sets diag(1/referenceNeutral), so the matrix is re-derived per temperature. That is what makes a profile track mixed lighting, and why the same Kelvin means a different rendering under a different profile.
- Exposure is preserved, which is why the control can be offered at all. The as-shot camera neutral is normalised to GREEN == 1 (CameraColor::asShotMul's convention) and the chain maps it to exactly (1,1,1). With a ForwardMatrix that is because a well-formed one has rows summing to the D50 white; without one, the adaptation is BUILT to carry the white the neutral lands on exactly onto D50. rawcolor.cpp anchors the same point the same way, so switching a raw onto a profile re-points its colour WITHOUT moving its brightness (a control that also nudged exposure would make one profile look "better" for the wrong reason). Pinned by tst_cameraprofile::neutralRendersNeutral (both paths, 1e-6) and ::profileChangeDoesNotMoveExposure.
- Measured on real data: over 416 ForwardMatrix rows from installed Adobe profiles, the worst deviation of a row sum from D50 is 3.0e-4, and the worst neutral error over 627 profile/temperature pairs is 3.9e-4 (about 2% of a 16-bit level, the rounding of rationals over 10000). So the exact assertions run on matrices row-normalised to D50 first (pinning THIS CODE), and a separate case runs on the published numbers bounded by their own deviation (pinning the real-data behaviour). One loose tolerance would stop detecting either.

Interpolation details that are easy to get wrong, all pinned:

- In MIRED (1/T), not in kelvin, as the spec requires. Halfway between 2856 K and 6504 K is 4680 K by kelvin but 3969 K by mired, and the second is the one that looks halfway.
- Warm first, by temperature, NOT in the order the file lists them. Adobe writes illuminant 1 = Standard A and 2 = D65, but nothing requires it, and a cool-first profile read in file order interpolates backwards.
- Clamped outside the two calibration temperatures (extrapolating a fitted matrix is not meaningful).
- ForwardMatrix is used only when BOTH calibrations have one; mixing a fitted forward matrix with a derived one would put a seam mid-range.
- A single-illuminant profile resolves at every temperature with weight 0.

Two shared pieces came out of this:

- ColorSpaceMath::adapt() (Bradford) and kWhiteD50 in Develop/colorspace.h. Every space in that header is D65 deliberately, so no chromatic adaptation hides in the ordinary pipeline; this is the ONE place a second white point is unavoidable, and nothing else should call it. The destination white is taken from the working space's own primaries (its RGB -> XYZ row sums), which is what makes a neutral land on exactly (1,1,1).
- WhiteBalance::illuminantXYZ() is public: the profile path keys its interpolation on the same illuminant definition the Temp slider uses (two loci, crossfaded, tint perpendicular), because two definitions of "6500 K" would disagree by a few hundred kelvin.

#### 11.6.4 Wiring

```
ImageFormats/Dcp           Dcp::peek()               read ONLY the two identifying strings
Develop/cameraprofilestore which profiles exist; hands out a parsed one
Develop/workingimage.h     CameraColor::cameraModel + ::profile
Develop/editparams.h       EditParams::cameraProfile (a NAME, not a path)
Develop/develop.cpp        Develop::InputMatrix: one definition of stage 0
Develop/workingimagecache  attachProfile(): the call site the feature hangs off
developproperties.cpp      the Profile row, its two greyed reasons, preset + multi-image
```

- The call site is in WorkingImageCache, not the decode. attachProfile() resolves the name against pixels ALREADY IN THE CACHE, every render. It clears the profile before resolving, so "no profile" cannot inherit the last one, and a name that no longer resolves leaves it null: the image renders with the built-in matrix, and the panel marks the name "(not installed)". It requires CameraNative pixels (see [10.4.1 Under the Apple Engine](#1041-under-the-apple-engine)) and re-solves the as-shot temperature for the profile (see [10.4.3 As Shot Is Profile-Dependent](#1043-as-shot-is-profile-dependent)).
- One definition of stage 0 (Develop::InputMatrix), shared by ToWorkingSpace and buildPointCoeffs's preMat fold, because the two must never disagree about which matrix an image went through. It returns the matrix AND whether it already carries the white balance.
- The white balance is applied EXACTLY ONCE, the least obvious rule in the feature. On the built-in path it is a per-channel gain in front of a fixed matrix; on the profile path it is diag(1/referenceNeutral) inside the matrix, so buildPointCoeffs drops the gains. It decides by testing img.cam.profile, NOT the image's space tag, because with an active local Denoise the conversion has already happened as its own pass and the tag no longer says where the pixels came from. Therefore ToWorkingSpace deliberately LEAVES cam.profile SET after converting; clearing it there (the tidy-looking thing) white-balances the image twice. Pinned by tst_inputprofile::cameraProfileSurvivesTheDenoiseRoute, mutation-checked.
- Stage 0 is spent after ONE Apply. The scope compositor develops each MASK LAYER by copying the base result and calling Apply again, and a WorkingImage copy carries `cam` wholesale. A profile left on the image would be spent again on every scope: the HueSatMap re-applied on itself, and (invisibly) the scope's OWN white balance dropped, since buildPointCoeffs reads cam.profile as "the white balance is already in the matrix" (true of the base, false of a layer above it). Develop::Apply CLEARS img.cam.profile when it finishes, and renderStack's RESUMED branch deliberately does not re-attach it (its prefix is already post-stage-0). Pinned by tst_inputprofile::stageZeroRunsOnlyOnce, mutation-checked.
- Stored BY NAME, not by path: the path differs per machine and per Adobe version, while the name plus the image's own camera model resolves it anywhere. It travels honestly in a preset and across a selection: it is resolved PER IMAGE against that image's model, so one camera's profile applied to another camera's raw simply does not resolve and is marked.
- A profile counts as an edit: cameraProfile is part of EditParams::isIdentity(), so choosing one makes the image non-identity (it renders, persists and shows the edited marker); the empty default keeps an untouched raw identity, writing no sidecar and leaving its devPreview key alone. paramsToJson OMITS the key when empty for the same reason.
- On a profile change, the stored Temp/Tint numbers are HELD and the rendering moves, as Lightroom does.

#### 11.6.5 Where Profiles Come From

Profiles are READ, never shipped. Adobe's .dcp files are licensed for use with Adobe products (ProfileCopyright, ProfileEmbedPolicy), so the store reads them where the user already has them. CameraProfileStore::roots(), in order: the machine-wide Adobe CameraProfiles folder (/Library/Application Support/Adobe/CameraRaw/CameraProfiles/ on macOS, the ProgramData path on Windows), the per-user one, and Winnow's own CameraProfiles folder under AppDataLocation. The user folder comes last, so a user-supplied profile of the same name does not displace an installed one in the menu; both appear. For a built-in default, keep the matrices the decoders already carry, or generate profiles with dcamprof (Anders Torger) or Adobe's DNG Profile Editor.

Implement from the DNG spec, not from source: RawTherapee's dcp.cc is GPL and must not be read into this codebase. The spec is public and complete; Adobe's own DNG SDK is permissively licensed if a reference implementation is wanted.

The index is built on a background thread, once per session. Measured: 4,373 installed profiles, 497 ms to read the two identifying strings from every one, against \~2.4 s to parse them fully (hence Dcp::peek, which touches no table). Half a second is under the one-second progress bar but over the bar for a dropdown that must not stall the GUI when a raw is opened, so the combo is filled with the built-in entry immediately and refilled when the sweep lands (CameraProfileStore::indexChanged). A stored but unresolved name is NOT marked "(not installed)" while the index is still building.

Still open: a preferences page for the profile folders (CameraProfileStore::roots() is public so a page can list them), and profiles embedded in a DNG (parseIfd is ready, nothing calls it).

#### 11.6.6 The HueSatMap

Develop/huesatmap.h, the table resolution in Develop/cameraprofile.cpp, the pass in Develop::ApplyProfileTables (stage 0.5); tests/unit/tst_huesatmap.cpp. The part a 3x3 cannot carry.

- The storage order is index = ((val \* hueDivs + hue) \* satDivs + sat) \* 3: value outermost, saturation innermost. Verified by two independent structural properties of real files: the saturation == 0 slice of all 279 installed HueSatMaps is EXACTLY (sat 1.0, val 1.0) under this order and deviates by up to 1.37 under the alternative (a profile that tinted greys would be unusable); and a real LookTable's value axis (the only tables with valDivs > 1) is smooth along this order's stride and \~8x rougher along the alternative's. The test then pins the order by construction, with a table whose entries encode their own indices.
- It runs in LINEAR ProPhoto RGB at D50, the space the spec names. The pixel is carried there and back by two folded 3x3s. ProPhoto is deliberately NOT added to ColorSpaceMath::ColorSpace (every space there is D65 by design); it lives in cameraprofile.cpp beside the one adaptation the pipeline allows.
- The destination white comes from ProPhoto's OWN matrix (its RGB -> XYZ row sums), NOT the published D50 triple. The two differ in the fourth decimal (0.96422 / 1 / 0.82521 against 0.9642 / 1 / 0.8249), and a neutral arriving 3e-4 off neutral has a non-zero SATURATION, so the identity slice is no longer the slice being read. Measured before the fix: real profiles tinted a neutral by 1.5e-4; after, 6e-8 (float epsilon). Pinned by tst_huesatmap::neutralSurvivesARealProfile, which also catches the bracketing matrices being wrong in either direction.
- The value axis is indexed CLAMPED and scaled UNCLAMPED, a deliberate departure from a literal reading of the spec. DNG describes a DISPLAY-REFERRED pipeline where value lives in 0..1; Winnow's working data is SCENE-REFERRED with stops of headroom above white. Clamping value would blow every specular highlight flat the moment a profile was selected. So a pixel above white is looked up at the top of the value axis and its value scale applied as a plain multiply. Saturation IS clamped to 0..1 (a value past 1 would produce a negative channel).
- The two illuminants' tables are blended once per render, not per pixel, with the same weight and warm-first order as the matrices (the interpolation is linear in the table values, so per-pixel sampling of both would double the eight-tap lookup for an identical result).
- An active HueSatMap forces the early conversion: a table cannot be folded into preMat, so the camera-native -> working conversion runs as its own pass first (as an active local Denoise also forces). The table runs BEFORE everything else, because it FINISHES the input profile; in particular it precedes Exposure, whose uniform scale does not commute with a table indexed by value. Develop::ProfileTablesActive means "has a HueSatMap" (a structural test, not a table build); a profile without one pays nothing.
- Measured (M4, 24 MP synthetic, Canon EOS 77D Adobe Standard, 90 x 30 x 1): 38-45 ms at full resolution and 5-6 ms at the 2.8 MP proxy an interactive drag renders.
- What is installed: 33 of \~120 sampled profiles carry a HueSatMap, all of the Adobe Standard family. Dimensions seen: 8x2x1, 36x10x1, 90x25x1, 90x30x1; valDivs is 1 on every installed HueSatMap, so they are effectively 2-D, while LookTables run to 90x16x16. An Adobe Standard rendering is finished by this stage; a "Camera Vivid" has no HueSatMap and its entire look lives in its LookTable.

#### 11.6.7 The Look Moved to the Output Stage

Since 2026-10-03, stage 0.5 applies ONLY the HueSatMap (the characterisation). The LOOK (LookTable, BaselineExposureOffset, ProfileToneCurve) is built into an OutputLook (Develop/outputlook.h), attached to WorkingImage::look (carried by copyMetadata; pinned by tst_inputprofile::lookSurvivesACopy), and OutputTransform applies it after every edit:

```
Profile curve    offset -> LookTable -> the profile's curve (with Winnow's roll-off)
anything else    offset -> LookTable -> offset undone -> the chosen tone mapping
```

- The offset is the exposure the look was BUILT at, so the LookTable always reads at it; it is undone for Winnow's own curves, which were fitted without it (Standard roll-off against Adobe Standard, offset 0).
- Mask scopes adjust BEFORE the look, as the SDK order implies (they used to adjust post-curve pixels).
- The curve is one of the tone mappings, never an override: ViewTransform::ProfileCurve (4). Every other choice renders the profile's COLOUR (matrices, HueSatMap, LookTable) under Winnow's tone, so Camera Vivid's grade with Standard roll-off is a real combination. "Profile curve" is greyed with "(none in this profile)" when the profile carries no curve, and EffectiveView renders it as Standard roll-off then.
- The curve is applied the SDK's way (RefBaselineRGBTone: curve the max and min channels, interpolate the middle), so hue is held and saturation follows the compression; and above a knee at output 0.60 the camera's shoulder is replaced by Winnow's power-law roll-off (Develop/cameracurve.h), so the curve keeps rising toward white past sensor white instead of extending linearly into a hard clip. ProfileTone (Develop/profiletone.h) was deleted; CameraCurve replaced it.
- BaselineExposureOffset is part of the look and travels with it: 224 of 436 sampled profiles carry a non-zero one, so omitting it would render most looks a fraction of a stop off. A "Camera Base" has it stripped, which keeps a base honest as a characterisation (colour, not brightness). The per-CAMERA BaselineExposure (tag 50730) in a .dcp is parsed and not applied; Winnow's per-camera baseline exposure comes from its own table (see [11.2.2 The Filmic Fit (kBaselineExposure and the Toe)](#1122-the-filmic-fit-kbaselineexposure-and-the-toe)).

What it replaced: the whole look used to run at stage 0.5, BEFORE exposure, in the order HueSatMap -> offset -> tone curve -> LookTable, the curve applied to VALUE and extended linearly above white, and a profile with a curve forced the view transform to None (WorkingImage::profileToneMapped; "set by the profile" in the panel). Two defects followed: Camera Neutral at +3 EV blew faces out to flat white (the curve had already carried the pixels to display white, then exposure multiplied them by 8), and the LookTable was read off post-curve data. The SDK's order is the reverse of what was built, so the old claim that the LookTable "was fitted against post-curve data" was wrong; verified against the SDK source, not recalled.

Winnow's look rendering is not bit-identical to Adobe's: Winnow's sliders are not ACR's, so the edits a look is applied over differ, and the curve's top end is Winnow's roll-off rather than the profile's own shoulder.

Performance (M4, 2.8 MP proxy; a real Sony "Camera VV", LookTable 90x16x16 sRGB-encoded, 128-point curve; measured with the look at stage 0.5, the per-pixel work is the same in OutputTransform's camera path):

```
matrix only (a Camera Base)       0.0 ms   the structural test skips the stage entirely
HueSatMap only (Adobe Standard)   5-6 ms
whole profile, as first written  21.4 ms
whole profile, after the fix     13.4 ms
```

The fix was the sRGB transfer, found by splitting the number rather than guessing: 247 of the 434 installed LookTables declare the sRGB encoding, and the round trip was SIX pow() calls per pixel. Forcing the transfer linear dropped 21.4 ms to 10.5, so the transfer was HALF the cost while the tone curve and value axis measured as free. Tabling it (16384 samples, linear reads) brought the real case to 13.4 ms, after which the tone curve measured \~3 ms, having been invisible behind it. The table size was measured too: 4096 samples give a worst error of 1.6e-5 (just over one 16-bit level); 16384 give 2.4e-6 for 131 KB and no measurable time.

#### 11.6.8 Camera Bases

A profile is applied WHOLE. Its bare characterisation is offered as its own dropdown entry, "Camera Base" (Develop/cameracurve.h, the look half of CameraProfile::tables, CameraProfileStore::deriveBases).

It was first built as a "Look" checkbox, and that was wrong. Recorded because the measurements that killed it justify what replaced it:

- Every "Camera \*" profile of one generation shares ONE colorimetric base: of 2,935 such profiles installed, only 42 carry a HueSatMap, and for a Sony ILCE-1M2 all nine v2 profiles are byte-identical with the look removed (as are all nine v1; the two generations differ). A per-profile "look off" switch turned nine rows into one unnamed rendering, including Camera BW, which is NOT MONOCHROME with its look off (the conversion lives entirely in its LookTable).
- A ProfileToneCurve is a whole tone mapping: Camera NT v2 maps scene-linear 0.18 to 0.478 (2.65x) with an end slope of 0.03, and 211 of 217 measured curves lift mid-grey by more than 1.5x. "Look off" was a profile with its tone mapping removed and nothing put back: dark, with clipped highlights.
- Lightroom has no such switch. It applies a profile whole, and where a profile carries no tone curve ACR supplies its own default (dng_tone_curve_acr3_default in the DNG SDK). Winnow's Tone mapping combo is the equivalent of that always-present curve, which is why Winnow has a state ACR does not: None, the unrendered picture.

"Camera Base" is a SYNTHESISED PROFILE, not a mode: CameraProfileStore hands back a Dcp::Profile copy with lookTable, toneCurve and baselineExposureOffset cleared, so the render path has no notion of a partly applied profile (EditParams gained no field, and CameraProfile::tables takes no flag).

- Selected by CONTENT: a profile contributes a base when its look carries a TONE CURVE. That picks out exactly the "Camera \*" family (Adobe Standard has a LookTable but zero curve points), keeps working for third-party profiles, and is the distinction that matters. Adobe Standard deliberately gets NO base: its look is a mild colour grade that measures as doing nothing on neutrals.
- One entry per distinct base, keyed on both matrix pairs, the per-unit calibration and the HueSatMap. 413 of 431 installed cameras yield exactly one, "Camera Base"; a camera shipping two generations (15 of them) gets "Camera Base" and "Camera Base v2", the suffix taken from what the group's member names share, cut back to a word boundary (otherwise "Camera ST" and "Camera NT" contribute a shared "T": "Camera BaseT"). A name that would collide falls back to appending a member's name, because profiles are resolved BY NAME and a duplicate would make one row unreachable.
- Derived lazily, per model, and cached. Grouping needs full parses, so it must NOT ride the \~0.5 s Dcp::peek index sweep. A camera has \~9-18 curve-bearing profiles, so deriving its bases costs \~10 ms once per camera per session, on the first forModel(). A base is cached under its source path plus a marker, never the bare path (it is a different profile from its file).

#### 11.6.9 Tests and Scope

tests/unit/tst_cameraprofile.cpp parses real .dcp files and pins tag values against a Python oracle for the byte layout (the raw decoders' libraw/rawpy pattern). The interpolation endpoints are pinned exactly (at each calibration illuminant's own temperature the interpolated matrix equals that illuminant's matrix), and so is the invariant that makes the whole thing trustworthy: a white-balanced camera neutral renders EXACTLY neutral after ForwardMatrix, for both illuminants and an interpolated point. Assert through ToImage16, not the 8-bit path: a mis-derived matrix lands inside a within-one tolerance at 8 bits.

Not in scope: ICC input profiles for non-raw wide-gamut files (a different mechanism; browsing handles them via ImageDecoder::colorManage); creative LUTs (see [11.7 Film-Look LUTs (.cube / HaldCLUT): Declined](#117-film-look-luts-cube--haldclut-declined)); per-individual-camera calibration (CameraCalibration1/2), which nobody without a target and a spectrophotometer can use.

### 11.7 Film-Look LUTs (.cube / HaldCLUT): Declined

NOT BUILT. This is a design record, not a description of the code. Film-look LUT support was written in full on 2026-09-14 (readers, store, render stage, UI and tests, all passing) and REMOVED the same day by the owner's decision: Winnow does not support .cube or HaldCLUT files, and nothing below exists in the tree. It is kept because the expensive parts were the decisions and the measurements, and a second attempt should start from them. The implementation is recoverable in git: commit 4491ed31 "Support cube files", reverted immediately after.

#### 11.7.1 The Design

- Why open formats, not Adobe's: Adobe's camera-matching looks (including every Fujifilm film simulation) are .xmp "Look" presets whose RGB table is base85 over an unidentified codec, proved not decodable from the files (see [10.8 Adobe Look Profiles (.xmp): Declined](#108-adobe-look-profiles-xmp-declined)). The open-source ecosystem solved the same job twice over with trivially readable formats, free Fuji film-simulation packs exist in both, and unlike Adobe's they work for EVERY camera.
- Two formats: .cube (IRIDAS/Adobe, plain text: LUT_3D_SIZE or LUT_1D_SIZE, optional TITLE and DOMAIN_MIN/MAX, then n^3 triplets) and HaldCLUT PNG (RawTherapee's: a level-L image is L^3 x L^3 pixels holding an L^2 cube). BOTH STORE RED FASTEST, so one indexer serves them and a transposition shows up as a red/blue swap. tst_lutparse emitted one analytic look as BOTH formats from one generator and required them to agree (a single transposed reader cannot pass), plus an eight-corner 2x2x2 cube as an independent second argument. The readers REJECTED rather than repaired (short, long, non-finite, oversized, degenerate domain): these are untrusted downloads, and a table quietly filled with zeros is a black picture nobody can explain.
- Where applied: inside OutputTransform, AFTER the transfer function, on display-referred sRGB, the encoding a LUT is authored against. Everything in Develop happens BEFORE the look: the adjustments are the exposure, the look is the stock they are printed on.
- Sandwiched into sRGB whatever the output space: working primaries -> linear sRGB -> sRGB transfer -> the LUT -> inverse sRGB transfer -> back. Applying it in whatever encoding the pixel is sitting in would make a P3 or Adobe RGB export read the table through the wrong primaries. Pinned by tst_outputtransform::lookIsAppliedInSrgbNotTheOutputSpace (mutation-checked: moving the call after the primaries matrix put it 96 counts out).
- Tetrahedral, not trilinear: on the grey axis the point lies on the cell's main diagonal, an edge shared by all six tetrahedra, so a look that keeps its greys neutral keeps them EXACTLY neutral. Trilinear blends eight corners, six off-axis, and tints every neutral a little. It is also four fetches against eight, and what Resolve, ACES and the .cube ecosystem do. tst_lut3d asserted both halves (tetrahedral holds the axis AND trilinear measurably does not).
- A look breaks the fused output path, deliberately: the fused table bakes the view curve and the transfer into ONE lookup and the look sits BETWEEN them. The no-look condition stayed byte-identical (tst_outputtransform::noLookOutputIsUnchanged). This does not repeal the outputtransform.cpp design note that the COLOUR-MANAGEMENT chain stays per-channel: a creative look is not expressible as matrices and 1-D curves; a 3-D table IS its definition.
- One row, mutually exclusive: camera profiles and looks shared the Profile combo in groups, and picking one cleared the other. The combo's ITEM DATA carried a kind prefix ("p:" / "l:") so one widget drove two parameters; the prefixes never reached a sidecar, preset or QSettings key. sanitizeParams repaired a stack naming both by keeping the LOOK.
- A look rendered on "Camera Base" where one exists (a .cube carries no sensor characterisation), falling back to the built-in matrix.
- The row stopped being raw-only: camera profiles still were, but a look is a creative grade on display-referred pixels, which is what a JPEG already is. So the profiles GROUP was absent there and the reason sat beside the live combo.
- The index key was the file's path under the Looks folder minus the extension ("Fuji/Classic Chrome"), not the .cube TITLE (missing or duplicated) and not the basename (two packs both ship a "Portra 400"); subfolders grouped the combo. It was resolved by LOOKUP, NEVER BY JOINING IT ONTO A ROOT: the key comes back out of a sidecar, which is user-editable text, so a store that built a path from it would hand "../../../etc/passwd" to QFile (tst_lutstore::keysCannotEscapeTheRoot).
- LutStore mirrored CameraProfileStore with one difference: lut() built the index SYNCHRONOUSLY when not built, because the raw decode path runs on a worker with no Develop panel behind it, and "not ready" would silently export without the look. Affordable for tens of files.
- Five call sites took the look (workingimagecache.cpp render() and renderStack(), and rawformat.cpp's three ToImage calls), and a defaulted nullptr meant a missed one rendered without it in silence. Weigh that fragility before rebuilding it the same way.
- The sidecar key was "lookLut", omitted when empty. It was ALSO the render-cache key: nothing in Develop::Apply read it, so paramsToJson was the only thing that made changing a look re-render (asserted in tst_lookparams). The retired key "cameraProfileLook" is unrelated and its name must never be reused.
- Installing (as designed): .cube or HaldCLUT .png files in a Looks folder beside the camera profiles folder, created on the first sweep, subfolders becoming groups. Many free .cube packs are authored for a LOG input (S-Log, LogC) rather than display-referred sRGB, and nothing in the file says which; that is a documentation problem, not a code one. Do NOT build auto-detection heuristics that guess.
- Not done, on purpose: an Amount/opacity slider (a later additive key; it cannot be retrofitted into lookLut's meaning); per-scope or masked looks (the look is applied after the scopes are composited, so it could not be per-scope even in principle); .3dl / .look / ICC; LUT export.

#### 11.7.2 Why One Row Was Right

The plan had said camera-matching profiles and creative looks must live in separate rows, because one answers "how is my sensor characterised" and the other "what grade is on top". That reasoning was not wrong, just outweighed: Adobe surfaces Adobe Raw / Camera / Artistic / B&W / Modern / Vintage in ONE browser, so the "conflation" is the convention every photographer reads; the user is asking one question at that moment ("what rendering is this picture?"), and two rows make them ask it twice; and the two are mutually exclusive, so one combo showing one selection is not a conflation (a second row would have shown "none" half the time). The confusion is answered by GROUPING inside the list. The argument applies again the moment anything other than a .dcp wants a place in that row.

#### 11.7.3 Cost, Measured

M4, 5.9 MP proxy, sRGB out, Filmic: toImage went from 2.4 ms with no look to 20.8 ms with one, an 18 ms addition to every interactive tick, NOT the "few ms" the plan estimated. Attribution (the obvious guesses were wrong twice): the split path instead of the fused one cost 3.1 ms; the 3-D sample only 2.0 ms (measured by swapping in a 1-D look); the remaining \~13 ms was THE sRGB SANDWICH, six tabulated transfer lookups per pixel whose branches also stopped the row loop vectorising. Rejected so nobody retries them: a 33^3 and a 64^3 table cost the same (not the table's size), and giving the sandwich its own smaller 4096-entry tables changed nothing (not cache eviction). Before measurement the code shipped std::pow in the sandwich (40 ms), then LutFor() inside the pixel loop, which takes a QMutex (431 ms), both found by benchmarking.

The optimisation not taken: for sRGB output with sRGB working primaries, the sandwich's outer halves are redundant (the view curve could be FUSED with the sRGB encode into one table, and the decode then cancels against the final transfer), leaving 3 lookups + the sample + the pack. It was not built: a fourth code path through the stage, helping only when the output space matches the working space. Build it when a measurement of a REAL Develop tick says the look is what hurts.

#### 11.7.4 What Survived the Removal

None of it is about looks: the mergePreset whole-image routing fix (cameraProfile and viewTransform had been written to the ACTIVE scope, so a preset applied while a mask scope was selected silently dropped them); RawTherapee's bundled dcpprofiles folder as a CameraProfileStore root (RawTherapee ships dual-illuminant DCPs and dcamprof emits standard ones, so the reader takes both unchanged: the cheapest way to widen coverage for makers Adobe serves thinly); tst_presetparams, the only test DevelopPresets::assignParam has; the separator under "Winnow Standard"; and tst_outputtransform::outputBytesAreUnchanged, the golden-hash gate over the whole output stage, which is what PROVED the removal restored OutputTransform byte for byte.

### 11.8 The Tone Controls

Blacks, Shadows, Highlights and Whites (Basic panel; the ToneRegionSlider bands; the Curves panel's Parametric view). Develop/develop.cpp, applyToneShape and the tone LUT built in buildPointCoeffs. The operators are FITTED to Lightroom Classic exports, not chosen.

#### 11.8.1 Two Kinds of Control

The question that started this was the wrong one, written down because it is the plausible one. Lightroom's histogram has FIVE draggable divisions (Blacks, Shadows, Exposure, Highlights, Whites) and Winnow's ToneRegionSlider has four bands, so the obvious theory is that the missing division explains why the tone sliders behaved differently. It does not: the missing one is EXPOSURE, which Winnow has (a scene-linear 2^EV gain folded into preMat at stage 3). Lightroom's histogram zone only drags that same global slider, and NEITHER APP HAS A MIDTONE REGION. The fifth division is a UI affordance that moves no pixels; it was deliberately left out (adding it would have made a behavioural change look like it was caused by a widget).

What actually differed was the shape of the operators: all four tone controls were the same operator (an additive Gaussian lift of the perceptual value, two of them pinned at s=0 and s=1) when they should have been two. Four defects, each measured on a 256-step perceptual ramp through Develop::Apply + OutputTransform::ToImage before anything changed (the numbers are tst_toneregions failing against the old code):

- Whites and Blacks were BUMPS, not endpoint moves. A Gaussian at s=1 brightens a BAND near white and can never move white itself. Lightroom's Whites and Blacks rescale where the curve REACHES white and black, so everything between moves with them. The discriminating measurement is reach at MID-GREY: Whites +100 moved mid-grey by 0 levels of 255 and Blacks +100 by 2.
- The regions STACKED instead of partitioning. The shadows and highlights lobes at 0.25 and 0.75 each carried \~38% of their weight at the crossover, so a midtone took both sliders IN FULL (39 levels for the pair against 19 and 20 alone), and Highlights -100 dragged white down 19 levels on its own.
- The composed curve could INVERT. Blacks +100 with Shadows -100 produced a locally decreasing LUT 20 samples into the ramp: a brighter input rendering darker than a dimmer one, a bright halo inside a smooth gradient (the failure Develop/tonecurve.h avoids with Fritsch-Carlson on the point curve).
- The regions slid with CONTRAST. The weights were sampled after the contrast slope, so raising Contrast moved the pixels Shadows and Highlights acted on (by 17 of 256 ramp samples at full contrast), while the handles draw those regions against the INPUT histogram.

The region handles were not where they were drawn (found by measurement). The weights were evaluated on Develop's working value, three stages upstream of the view transform, while the handles are drawn under the histogram scope, which shows the FINISHED render. Under Filmic the three handles at 0.25 / 0.50 / 0.75 acted at display levels 67 / 170 / 236, so Highlights began above level 170, above most of most pictures; that, not its amplitude, is why it barely did anything (peaking at -17 levels where Lightroom peaks at -59). The weights are now evaluated through OutputTransform::DisplayPosition (the perceptual value through the view transform and transfer function, the chain ToImage runs). With that alone, Highlights -100 went from -17 to -60 levels against Lightroom's -59.
